II. 
Purpose of Testimony 
4 
Q. 
What is the purpose of the Panel’s testimony?  
5 
A. 
The purpose of the Panel’s testimony is to present the Company’s plans for 
6 
electric system capital investment and operations and maintenance 
7 
(“O&M”) activities, as well as to describe the primary drivers affecting the 
8 
investment and operations plans for the period covered by this rate case 
9 
filing.  The Panel describes: (1) historic capital spending for the period from 
10 
fiscal year (“FY”) 2016 through FY20, and (2) planned capital spending for 
11 
FY21 through FY25.  The Rate Year is the twelve months ending June 30, 
12 
2022.  Data Year 1 is the twelve months ending June 30, 2023.  Data Year 2 
13 
is the twelve months ending June 30, 2024.  Data Year 1 and Data Year 2 
14 
are collectively referred to as the “Data Years.”  This information is 
15 
summarized in Exhibit __ (EIOP-2).  
16 
 
17 
With respect to capital investments, the Panel’s testimony provides a 
18 
detailed description of the electric infrastructure investment plan for the 
19 
period FY21 – FY25, and a comparison of prior capital investment amounts.  
20 
The Panel also describes the Company’s methodology to develop its 
21 


--- Page 13 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 11 of 127 
 
investment plans, prioritize its budget and annual work plan, and execute 
1 
that work plan.  The capital plan presented in the Company’s filing reflects 
2 
the investments necessary to maintain reliability, continue to increase 
3 
system resiliency,  enable a sustainable energy infrastructure as envisioned 
4 
under New York’s Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act of 
5 
2019 (“CLCPA”) and the Accelerated Renewable Energy Growth and 
6 
Community Benefit Act, and enable a more animated, dynamic energy 
7 
marketplace that will ultimately deliver greater value and benefits for 
8 
customers.     
9 
 
10 
Q. 
How has the Company presented its projected capital and O&M 
11 
expenditures in the case? 
12 
A. 
As the Revenue Requirements Panel explains in its testimony, the Company 
13 
operates on a FY that runs from April 1 through March 31, and typically 
14 
develops its capital and expense budgets on an FY basis.  Because of the 
15 
delay in filing this rate case related to the COVID-19 pandemic, the 
16 
proposed Rate Year and Data Years do not directly align with the 
17 
Company’s FY budgeting period.  Unless otherwise specifically indicated, 
18 
the capital project and program costs described in our testimony are 
19 
presented as FY costs.   
20 
 
21 


--- Page 14 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 12 of 127 
 
 
To present the Rate Year and Data year revenue requirements reflected in 
1 
this case, the Company used the FY capital plan forecasts and cashed flow 
2 
them based on historic spending patterns to develop rate year schedules 
3 
presented in the exhibits of the Revenue Requirements Panel.   
4 
 
5 
            The Company’s projected O&M expenditures also have been converted to 
6 
Rate Year and Data Year amounts and are represented that way in relevant 
7 
exhibits and the revenue requirement. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
What are some of the key areas of focus presented in the Panel’s 
10 
testimony? 
11 
A. 
The Company’s electric infrastructure and operations plan is designed to 
12 
achieve continued safe and reliable service in the face of a changing climate 
13 
and volatile weather, and modernize and enhance the grid to promote the 
14 
transition to a sustainable energy future, all while balancing the impacts on 
15 
customer bills.  A substantial proportion of the Company’s planned spend is 
16 
targeted at traditional areas needed for continued safe and reliable service 
17 
(e.g., asset condition investment, reliability and resiliency programs).  In 
18 
addition, like the rest of society and the economy, the electric system relies 
19 
increasingly on advanced communications and information technologies.  
20 
The Panel’s testimony therefore also describes several communications and 
21 


--- Page 15 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 13 of 127 
 
IT investments that are necessary to support the evolving needs of 
1 
customers and the increasing complexity of the modernized grid.  Some of 
2 
the investment areas the Company is proposing are relatively new for the 
3 
electric utility industry (e.g., electric vehicle (“EV”) related spending; 
4 
energy storage systems (“ESS”); multi-value transmission (“MVT”); Fault 
5 
Location Isolation and Service Restoration (“FLISR”); transmission 
6 
resiliency). 
7 
 
8 
The Panel’s proposed investment plan assumes that certain enabling 
9 
investments also are implemented.  In particular, the Company’s investment 
10 
plan includes amounts for advanced metering infrastructure (“AMI”) 
11 
implementation, the details of which are described in the direct testimony 
12 
of the AMI Panel.   
13 
 
14 
The investment plans presented in the exhibits to the Panel’s testimony also 
15 
include other capital investments essential to running the business, 
16 
including facilities and properties, information technology systems, fleet 
17 
assets, and investments to support the inventory management and 
18 
warehouse management (“IM/WM”) including investment recovery 
19 
functions.  The testimony support for such investments is provided in the 
20 
direct testimony of the Company’s Shared Services Panel and IT Panel.    
21

Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 14 of 127 
 
With respect to O&M activities, the Panel’s testimony summarizes the 
1 
Company’s ordinary O&M activities and costs, and describes, in detail, a 
2 
number of programs the Company proposes to implement in the Rate Year, 
3 
the costs of which are not fully reflected in the twelve months ended 
4 
December 31, 2019 (“Historic Test Year”).  These programs represent 
5 
incremental, known, and measurable changes from Historic Test Year 
6 
expense, and include, among other things, focused programs to address 
7 
Spier-Rotterdam tower painting, enhanced 3A/3B transmission tower 
8 
inspections, light detection and ranging/aerial laser surveys, and increased 
9 
vegetation management costs.  In addition, the Panel describes shifting 
10 
trends in the contractor market for skilled line and technical resources 
11 
leading to incremental field resource requirements needed to implement the 
12 
Company’s work plan.   
13 
 
14 
The Company continues to provide strong restoration response to the 
15 
volatile weather events impacting our customers.  This Panel’s testimony 
16 
proposes updates to the mechanisms utilized to track, classify, and recover 
17 
costs associated with response efforts for both major and minor storm 
18 
events.   
19 
 
20

10 
Q. 
Please explain the objectives of the electric infrastructure investment 
11 
and operations plans presented in this filing. 
12 
A. 
The Company’s electric infrastructure and operations plans are developed 
13 
to  provide customers with safe and reliable service at reasonable costs, and 
14 
to do so while continuing to modernize the grid as part of our core 
15 
responsibility to meet the changing needs of our customers, stakeholders, 
16 
and the environment.  It includes a commitment to introducing programs 
17 
and projects specifically designed to meet clean energy goals, such as those 
18 
presented in the CLCPA.  
19 
 
20 


--- Page 20 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 18 of 127 
 
The Company’s electric service territory encompasses approximately 
1 
25,000 square miles in more than 450 cities and towns and serves 
2 
approximately 1.65 million customers.  In addition to building 
3 
infrastructure to meet new customer needs, the Company’s investment plan 
4 
also addresses the needs of the existing infrastructure. The Company’s 
5 
system is comprised of over 6,000 circuit miles of transmission lines, more 
6 
than 200 transmission substations, over 3,200 circuit miles of sub-
7 
transmission lines, over 500 distribution substations, more than 711 large 
8 
power transformers, approximately 44,000 circuit miles of primary 
9 
distribution line supplying over 410,000 line transformers, with over 1.2 
10 
million distribution poles and many more assets.   
11 
 
12 
A significant number of these assets have been in service for 70 years or 
13 
more, and exhibit conditions consistent with their age.  In many cases, such 
14 
equipment can no longer be effectively maintained because of 
15 
obsolescence.  Attention to these assets is essential to continued reliable 
16 
operation and resiliency of the system.  Addressing these concerns is a core 
17 
objective, and hence asset condition accounts for a significant portion of the 
18 
work presented in this case.  
19 
 
20 


--- Page 21 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 19 of 127 
 
In summary, the Company’s overall objective is to develop cost-effective 
1

2 
customers, maintain the integrity and reliability of the system, and continue 
3 
the transition to a more advanced, resilient, and sustainable electric system

to deliver increasing levels of clean energy to customers.

Q. 
How has the COVID-19 pandemic affected the Company’s capital 
1 
investment and O&M plans? 
2 
A. 
Measures taken by New York State to protect public health were among the 
3 
most comprehensive in the country, and have proven to be very effective in 
4 
reducing the spread of the coronavirus and “flattening the curve.”  Because 
5 
utility construction was identified as “essential” under the COVID-19 
6 
guidelines, the Company has continued to deliver the vast majority of its 
7 
planned capital investment work during the lockdown.  The Company’s 
8 
field force has been working in accordance with the guidance and directives 
9 
for maintaining a clean and safe work environment issued by the 
10 
Department of Health.  For on-site construction, this includes maintaining 
11 
social distance and limiting worksites to only those workers required to 
12 
support essential business activities, with no other employees or personnel 
13 
allowed at the site.  The Company also modified its work plans to limit 
14 
planned interruptions and outages that increased Load at Risk (LAR) in late 
15 
March, and stopped work inside of customers’ homes.  As a result, customer 
16 
impacts have been mitigated and the Company has been able to deliver the 
17 
essential work plan and maintain overall capital investment levels in the 
18 
period following the lockdown near its planned investment levels for the 
19 
period.   
20 
 
 
21

Q. 
Does the Company anticipate any long-term impacts from the 
1 
pandemic on its investment plans? 
2 
A.  
Local economies in areas served by the Company experienced significant 
3 
immediate impacts following implementation of the public health measures.  
4 
With many companies reducing or suspending operations since the start of 
5 
the lockdown, and many more people being home during the traditional 
6 
work week, the Company has seen less overall demand, and also shifts in 
7 
load; i.e., increased residential load and decreased commercial and 
8 
industrial demand during the week.  Although the pandemic has reduced 
9 
and shifted load, and reduced the Company’s near-term investment levels 
10 
relative to those presented in the CIP, the long-term need for investment in 
11 
the system continues, and the Company anticipates that capital investment 
12 
levels will approximate previously envisioned levels within the next one to 
13 
two years to address system needs.   
14 
 
15 
 
Thus, the investment plan presented here reflects lower near-term 
16 
investment levels—primarily in the area of new business connections and 
17 
services—however, the Company expects that to turn around in the next 
18 
few years.  Further, the Company does not expect that the pandemic will 
19 
have significant lasting impacts on workforce resourcing; and, to date, the 
20 
Company has not seen any supply chain impacts that have negatively

B. 
Capital Plan Budgeting 
13 
Q. 
Please describe the development of the Company’s capital plan. 
14 
A. 
The Company’s capital plan is developed and prioritized to achieve the 
15 
objectives described in testimony above.  Projects are categorized by the 
16 
spending rationales, and proposed spending includes the latest cost 
17 
estimates for in-progress projects as well as initial estimates for newly 
18 
proposed projects.  Expected deviations from historic trends, volume, and 
19 
cost of work are also considered. 
20 
 
21 


--- Page 28 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 26 of 127 
 
All mandatory projects known at the time are included in the plan.  Once 
1 
the budget level has been established for mandatory work, projects in the 
2 
other spending rationales are reviewed for inclusion in the plan.  The 
3 
decision whether to include a project in the plan is based on several factors 
4 
including, but not limited to, whether the project is new or in-progress, risk 
5 
score, customer impacts, and resource availability.   
6 
 
7 
The plan is reviewed with the President of the New York jurisdiction and 
8 
the Finance organization.  The New York President reviews the overall 
9 
customer, service quality, and financial impacts of the investment plan as 
10 
part of the business planning process and may request changes to the level 
11 
or combination of investments.   
12 
 
13 
A corporate plan is then presented to the National Grid plc Executive 
14 
Committee.  The capital portfolio is subsequently presented to the National 
15 
Grid plc Board of Directors for review and approval.  The budget amount is 
16 
approved on the basis that it meets the business objectives set for that year.  
17 
The result of the budgeting process is the approval of the capital spending 
18 
plan for the budget year. 
19 
 
20 


--- Page 29 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 27 of 127 
 
Q. 
Are there additional approvals needed before a project or program in 
1 
the annual capital plan can proceed? 
2 
A. 
Yes.  Aside from the capital planning and budgeting process, specific 
3 
approval must be obtained for any project or programs within the five-year 
4 
capital plan to proceed.  Approval is obtained through the US Capital 
5 
Sanctioning Process.  All projects and programs greater than $8 million are 
6 
reviewed for approval by the US Sanctioning Committee (“USSC”), a 
7 
committee established by the National Grid USA Board of Directors for this 
8 
purpose.  Projects or programs estimated at greater than $25 million and 
9 
less than or equal to $203 million are reviewed and approved by the Senior 
10 
Executive Sanctioning Committee (“SESC”).  Projects greater than $203 
11 
million are approved by the plc Executive Board. Other projects and 
12 
programs from $1 million to $8 million are approved by the Vice President 
13 
Service Company Finance Business Partner and are considered by the 
14 
USSC through that committee’s consent agenda process.  Projects less than 
15 
$1 million are approved through a supervisory hierarchy based on certain 
16 
established delegated authority thresholds.   
17

20 
forecast the Rate Year and Data Years.

--- Page 30 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel

A. 
The timing of the sanctioning process is not aligned with the capital 
1 
planning process used to forecast the Rate Year and Data Years.  The 
2 
Company develops a long-term investment plan that is used as the basis for 
3 
the forecast for the Rate Year, Data Year 1, and Data Year 2 proposals.  
4 
Sanctioning, however, takes place through an on-going process as unique 
5 
projects progress through their life cycle.  Additionally, most major 
6 
programs of work are sanctioned just prior to the fiscal year for which the 
7 
investment is planned.  For example, FY22 capital programs generally will 
8 
be sanctioned in early 2021.  Thus, the Rate Year and Data Years include 
9 
conceptual and partially sanctioned projects.

its capital portfolio to account for changes in project schedules, scopes, and 
4 
priorities, and addresses such changes in a manner to assure continued safe 
5 
and reliable service for customers at reasonable cost.

Q.

20 


--- Page 58 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 56 of 127 
 
The OpTel investment is a suite of efforts designed to address existing 
1 
business needs while creating a foundation upon which to build future 
2 
capabilities and services for customers.  The Company will upgrade and 
3 
expand the current communications infrastructure to provide near real-time 
4 
situational awareness and control of remote assets and support field use 
5 
cases like Substation Automation, Teleprotection, Physical Security, 
6 
Distribution Automation (DA) technologies (e.g., VVO, FLISR, sensors, 
7 
etc.), AMI, SCADA, DER integration, and customer substation 
8 
connectivity.  The Optel network consists of four tiers and utilizes multiple 
9 
wired and wireless communications technologies.   
10 
• Tier 1 - provides the network core with high bandwidth, fully 
11 
redundant, fiber based capacity connecting our major facilities and 
12 
substations.   
13 
• Tier 2 - expands the network to smaller facilities and substations 
14 
using fiber, high capacity microwave links and other private licensed 
15 
Point-to-Multi-Point (PtMP) radio frequency communications.    
16 
• Tier 3 - extends the network to end devices at small substations and 
17 
on the distribution grid using various wireless technologies.     
18 
• Tier 4 - supports facility area networks for services such as Home 
19 
Energy Management Systems (HMS), demand response, residential 
20 
and commercial DER, and Smart City capabilities.    
21 


--- Page 59 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 57 of 127 
 
 
The investments included in this rate filing cover the first phase of the plan, 
1 
which is focused on building a solid Tier 1 and Tier 2 foundation necessary 
2 
to support the OpTel infrastructure.  Tiers 1 and 2 work in concert to create 
3 
what is referred to as the Wide Area Network (WAN).  Elements of the first-
4 
phase include:   
5 
(i) 
Replacing obsolete data multiplexer (“DMX”) equipment on remote 
6 
ends of existing fiber infrastructure; this equipment is no longer 
7 
supported and technologically obsolete.  The replacement system 
8 
will provide enhanced capability and capacity while increasing 
9 
security and providing operational improvements. 
10 
(ii)

A. Non-Wires Alternatives 
16 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s approach to incorporating NWAs into 
17 
electric system planning.    
18 
A. 
The Company continues to improve its methods of integrating NWAs into 
19 
the system planning process. The system planning process can be broken 
20 
into three essential steps: (i) identify and quantify needs, (ii) develop 
21 


--- Page 63 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 61 of 127 
 
solution options to meet needs, and (iii) select an optimal solution that will 
1 
move into project implementation and delivery.  NWAs are integrated at the 
2 
first step, where planners consider how to quantify needs in novel ways to 
3 
better evaluate NWA options through the remainder of the system planning 
4 
process.  NWAs are considered in parallel with traditional options, utilizing 
5 
the NWA Suitability Criteria. Ultimately, the goal of this process is to 
6 
integrate NWAs as another tool in planners’ tool boxes and create an 
7 
understanding of how to best take advantage of the technical, economic, and 
8 
environmental benefits an NWA can provide customers in place of or in 
9 
concert with a traditional wires-solution. These process improvements have 
10 
been developed in collaboration with DPS Staff, whose input has been 
11 
shared with the Joint Utilities (“JU”) through various JU working groups. 
12 
Timelines and processes for traditional capital delivery and NWA 
13 
solicitation and implementation have been fully integrated, meaning 
14 
evaluating and delivering NWAs has become ‘business as usual’ for 
15 
National Grid.   
16

Q. 
How does the Company determine if a proposed NWA is beneficial 
4 
compared to a traditional capital investment solution? 
5 
A. 
The Company performs a BCA of the NWA using the Benefit Cost Analysis 
6 
Handbook Version 3.0 (“BCA Handbook”) adopted in Case 16-M-0412 and 
7 
compares the present value of the NWA solution benefits with the present 
8 
value of the traditional capital investment solution.  The difference in the 
9 
two present values represents the initial net benefit to society for the NWA 
10 
project.

Q.  
Please describe the ADMS project. 
1 
A. 
An Advanced Distribution Management System (“ADMS”) is a suite of 
2 
control room-based hardware and software tools used by electric 
3 
distribution operators to visualize, monitor, and control the electric grid.  
4 
Advanced applications in the software incorporate real time grid status and 
5 
measurements on an as-operated network model to help optimize 
6 
operational decisions and processes.  The ADMS supports continued safe 
7 
and reliable electric grid operations with the added complexities of the 
8 
modern grid such as DERs, EVs and other technologies. 
9 
 
 
10 
 
The ADMS system includes three main modules: A Distribution 
11 
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (“DSCADA”), an Outage 
12 
Management System (“OMS”) and advanced applications Distribution 
13 
Management System (“DMS”).   
14 
 
15 
 
The system can help the control room operator make more optimal system 
16 
configuration decisions with respect to power aspects of the grid by 
17 
enabling bi-directional load flow solutions incorporating data from remote 
18 
metering and simulating future configurations during emergency and 
19 
planned work. ADMS Applications can also centralize and automate 
20 
distribution grid functions such as volt var optimization (“VVO”) and 
21 


--- Page 77 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 75 of 127 
 
remote switching, as well as adding efficiencies to control room functions 
1 
such as switch order creation. The ADMS is a critical platform supporting 
2 
the operational integration of DER and is a foundational investment of the 
3 
Distributed System Platform (“DSP”). 
4 
 
5 
 
The Company is confident that this project will meet the needs described 
6 
above because of the ADMS investigation already performed.  Capabilities 
7 
and requirements have been defined and system design for the first phase of 
8 
ADMS implementation is complete.  A thorough analysis of operational 
9 
processes affected by the implementation of an ADMS has been conducted 
10 
along with a review of change impacts and training requirements. This will 
11 
ensure the solutions fit as designed into operations, is properly adopted, and 
12 
delivers expected benefits. 
13 
 
14

of CY 2021 – CY 2024.  The first phase of the ADMS project will put 
18 
distribution management system applications in service to be utilized by the 
19

20 
requirements and design stage of the project started in spring of 2019 and 
21 


--- Page 78 ---

D. 
In-Service Dates  
8 
Q. 
What is the effect of the in-service date of a project on the Company’s 
9 
revenue requirements? 
10 
A. 
The in-service date of a project determines when a project is reflected in the 
11 
Company’s rate base for depreciation purposes.    
12 
 
13 
Q. 
Please explain how the Company determines the in-service dates for 
14 
planned electric capital spending. 
15 
A. 
First, the Company’s objective is to establish in-service dates that accurately 
16 
reflect the estimated actual in-service date.  The ability to accurately 
17 
estimate in-service dates for large projects that are already underway and 
18 
near completion is obviously greater than for projects that have not 
19 
commenced and are further out in time.  Larger projects are also often 
20 
subject to licensing and permitting requirements, which can increase 
21 


--- Page 80 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 78 of 127 
 
complexity and often lead to changes in scope and implementation 
1 
schedules.   
2 
 
3 
            It is even more challenging to  predict the future in-service dates of smaller 
4 
projects and programmatic work, which will be shorter in cycle and more 
5 
prone to schedule shifts for reasons such as operational efficiency or the 
6 
need to address more urgent customer work.   
7 
 
8 
Therefore, in developing the in-service dates reflected in this case, the 
9 
Company estimates actual in-service dates for very large projects (i.e., those 
10 
with estimated costs greater than $10 million).  For the remaining programs 
11 
and projects, the Company developed closing rules pursuant to accounting 
12 
closing processes applicable to the type of project or program.  Thus, 
13 
amounts for construction work in progress (“CWIP”) and capital 
14 
expenditure cash flows forecast from CWIP were estimated to go into 
15 
service in the month following the applicable period under the closing rule.  
16 
The relevant closing rule periods were determined based on a historical 
17 
analysis of CWIP and plant closings, along with considering the future 
18 
capital project mix.  Sample closing periods used by the Company include: 
19 
transmission substations and distribution substations—twelve months; 
20 
transmission lines—seven months; distribution lines—six months; general 
21 


--- Page 81 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 79 of 127 
 
plant—three months; street lighting—three months; meters and line 
1 
transformers—one month.  For example, assuming a projected expenditure 
2 
of $100,000 in January for a distribution line capital project, the expenditure 
3 
would be deemed closed to plant in service in the month following the 
4 
closing rule period, or July.    
5

E. 
Cost of Removal 
7 
Q. 
Does the Company’s revenue requirement in this case include cost of 
8 
removal (“COR”) associated with the capital investment plan?   
9 
A. 
Yes.  In addition to the capital costs discussed above, there is a level of COR 
10 
required to implement the Company’s infrastructure investment plan.  As 
11 
reflected in Exhibit __ (EIOP-3), the Company forecasts COR of 
12 
approximately $73 million in FY21, $60 million in FY22, $65 million in 
13 
FY23, $72 million in FY24, and $72 million in FY25.   
14 
 
15 
Q. 
What types of activities are associated with COR? 
16 
A. 
The Company defines removal as any work on an existing capital asset that 
17 
results in the asset being removed from the asset inventory, whether a 
18 
different asset is subsequently added in its place.  This type of work would 
19 
include, but is not limited to, all the activities associated with disconnection, 
20 
removal and disposal of capital units of property such as circuit breakers 
21 


--- Page 82 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 80 of 127 
 
and transformers; disconnection, removal and disposal of secondary items 
1 
of equipment such as relays and control equipment; removal and/or 
2 
demolition of foundations; disconnection, removal and disposal of insulator 
3 
strings; removal of wood poles or steel structures; and disconnection and 
4 
removal of conductor and shield wire. 
5 
 
6 
Q.  
Please explain the basis for the forecast COR amounts. 
7 
A.  
COR is dependent on the nature of the project.  New construction projects 
8 
with limited impact on existing facilities typically have no, or relatively low, 
9 
COR forecasts.  Conversely, projects that involve replacement of substantial 
10 
portions of existing facilities would have relatively high COR forecasts.  In 
11 
addition, the type of work affects COR; for example, line projects typically 
12 
have higher COR than substation projects.  Some projects, such as the 
13 
removal of de-energized lines that have been determined to be of no future 
14 
beneficial use, are COR-only projects.  Thus, the COR in the investment 
15 
plan will vary depending on the nature and amount of work in the plan.  The 
16 
COR in this filing is based on the forecast removal associated with the 
17 
specific projects included in the plan.   
18 
 
19 
Q. 
How does the forecast COR compare to historic COR levels? 
20 


--- Page 83 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 81 of 127 
 
A. 
Comparison of historic and forecast COR as a percentage of capital 
1 
investment levels is provided in Revenue Requirements Panel Exhibit __ 
2 
(RRP-11), Workpapers for Exhibit (RRP-7), Schedule 1, Workpapers 15 and 
3 
16.  In general, historic and forecast COR percentages are fairly close.  In 
4 
those cases where forecast and historic COR percentages differ 
5 
substantially, such differences are due to the different nature of the capital 
6 
work (e.g., new versus replacement, line versus substation, etc.).

13

14

16

17 
1000 requires the creation of a planning process at regional independent 
18

20 
2015, the New York Independent System Operator’s (“NYISO”) Public 
21 


--- Page 85 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel

2 
York transmission market to competition.

5 
several public policy proceedings to identify potential projects to address 
6 
Public Policy Transmission Needs (“PPTN”).  These proceedings included

B. 
Vegetation Management  
10 
Q.  
Please describe the Company’s vegetation management program. 
11 
A. 
The Company’s vegetation management program is divided into three sub-
12 
programs: distribution, sub-transmission, and transmission.  Each program 
13 
includes a cycle-based component and a reliability improvement component 
14 
to minimize interruptions from trees and limbs falling into the 
15 
infrastructure, and to provide greater public and worker safety.   
16 
 
17 
For the sub-transmission and transmission systems, work is organized into 
18 
two components: a floor component and a sideline hazard/danger tree 
19 
component.  The floor work is cycle-based and is managed by integrated 
20 
vegetation management (“IVM”).  The sideline component is focused on 
21 


--- Page 97 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 95 of 127 
 
danger/hazard trees which are prioritized and scheduled based on a host of 
1 
variables. 
2 
 
  
3 
The Company’s distribution cycle-based component is circuit pruning, a 
4 
comprehensive program that provides for the pruning of vegetation along 
5 
all distribution circuit miles on an average five and a half year interval or 
6 
cycle.  An optimal cycle length is set for each circuit based on growing 
7 
season, growth characteristics of predominant tree species in that area, and 
8 
the appropriate clearance to be created at the time of pruning.  The Company 
9 
has maintained the appropriate level of funding necessary to operate the 
10 
program for many years allowing the completion of multiple full cycles of 
11 
pruning, which have been instrumental in the Company’s ability to provide 
12 
reliable service to its customers.  In addition to the routine pruning, hazard 
13 
tree removals are performed on prioritized distribution feeders.  The 
14 
Company identifies feeders for the inspection and removal of hazard trees 
15 
based on field inspections, tree exposure, historical interruption data, 
16 
number of customers served, and circuit configuration. 
17 
  
18 
Q. 
How much is the Company proposing to spend on vegetation 
19 
management? 
20 


--- Page 98 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 96 of 127 
 
A.

L. 
Annual Major Storm Recovery  
17 
Q. 
Is the Company proposing any changes to its storm cost recovery 
18 
mechanism? 
19 
A. 
Yes.  The Company proposes to: (i) adopt the definition of “major storm” 
20 
in Commission Rule 97.1(c) for purposes of determining cost recovery and 
21 


--- Page 115 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 113 of 127 
 
deferral eligibility; (ii) implement a two-way reconciliation mechanism for 
1 
minor storm costs; and (iii) establish a deferral mechanism for pre-staging 
2 
costs for storm events that do not meet the definition of a major storm. 
3 
 
4 
Q. 
Why is the Company proposing to adopt the regulatory definition of 
5 
“major storm” for determining cost recovery and deferral eligibility? 
6 
A.  
Currently, the Company is permitted to defer the cost of a storm event if  10 
7 
percent or more of customers in a region are interrupted, or 1 percent or 
8 
more of  customers in a region are interrupted for 24 hours or longer.  This 
9 
standard is different from the definition of a “major storm” used for 
10 
purposes of calculating the Company’s reliability performance.  For 
11 
assessing reliability performance, the Company uses the definition from the 
12 
Commission’s Rule 97.1(c), which provides that “[a] major storm is a 
13 
period of adverse weather during which service interruptions affect at least 
14 
10 percent of the customers in an operating area and/or result in customers 
15 
being without electric service for durations of at least 24 hours.”  The 
16 
Company’s proposal is to use a common definition of “major storm” for 
17 
reliability assessment and deferral eligibility, which will simplify 
18 
administration and avoid confusion caused by the current different 
19 
definitions used for calculating reliability and determining eligibility for 
20 
cost recovery. 
21 


--- Page 116 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 114 of 127 
 
Q. 
Why does the Company have different definitions for “major storm” in 
1 
place currently? 
2 
A. 
The current definition of “major storm” for deferral purposes was 
3 
established in 2007 as part of a settlement in several proceedings.  Section 
4 
3.6.1 of the Stipulation of the Parties dated March 22, 2007, in Cases 01-
5 
M-0075, 01-E-0011, 04-M-0159, 04-M-0938 and 07-M-0173 (“Second 
6 
CTC Reset Stipulation” or “Stipulation”) provides in part that:  
7 
 
“Only for purposes of the deferral of costs under Section 1.2.4.5 of 
8 
the Merger Joint Proposal, a period of adverse weather shall be 
9 
considered a “Major Storm” if: (a) service interruptions affect at 
10 
least 10 percent of the customers in an operating area; and/or (b) 
11 
service interruptions result in at least 1 percent of the customers in 
12 
an operating area being without electric service for durations of at 
13 
least 24 hours.” 
14 
 
A footnote to this language in the Stipulation provides that “[f]or operational 
15 
purposes, the criteria for determining whether a storm is classified as major 
16 
remains unchanged.”   Thus, the Second CTC Reset Stipulation created the 
17 
distinction between the definition of “major storm” for reliability and cost 
18 
deferral purposes.   
19 
 
20 


--- Page 117 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 115 of 127 
 
Q. 
Why is the Company proposing to eliminate the distinction created in 
1 
Stipulation?   
2 
A. 
The requirement that service be interrupted to at least one percent of 
3 
customers in a region for a storm to qualify for cost deferral was presumably 
4 
adopted over concerns that potentially small weather events could qualify 
5 
for cost deferral if even just a small number of customers were without 
6 
service for 24 hours or more.  The Company’s significant commitment to 
7 
service restoration for any customer whose service is impacted by weather 
8 
events, or for any other reason, is consistent and has been clearly displayed 
9 
independently of the number of customers impacted at a given time.  At the 
10 
same time, the standard for measuring reliability performance on behalf of 
11 
customers, including subsequent penalties for under performance, uses the 
12 
major storm definition in Section 97.1(c) of the Commission’s regulations 
13 
(16 NYCRR 97.1(c)).  In the Company’s view, there is no reason for 
14 
maintaining two different standards. 
15 
 
In addition, the increased complexity of having two criteria creates 
16 
confusion and leads to unnecessarily complex and burdensome 
17 
administration, tracking and review of storm costs.   
18 
 
19 
 
Finally, the definition distinction adopted in 2007 was intended to apply 
20 
through the period covered by the rate plan in Case 01-M-0075.  Indeed, 
21 


--- Page 118 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 116 of 127 
 
Section 3 of the Second CTC Reset Stipulation—in which the definitional 
1 
difference was created—is entitled “Stipulations As To Deferrals From July 
2 
1, 2005 – December 31, 2011.”  Since the Stipulation was adopted, the 
3 
Commission has considered and acted upon three complete rate case filings 
4 
by the Company.  The conditions and circumstances that may have existed 
5 
that led to the 2007 Stipulation are not the same today, and certainly do not 
6 
warrant differential treatment of the definition of major storms.  Therefore, 
7 
the Company proposes to adopt a common definition of “major storm” to 
8 
be when an adverse weather event results in at least 10 percent of customers 
9 
in a region being interrupted, or customers being interrupted for 24 hours or 
10 
longer.  The Company’s forecast for major storm expenses reflect this 
11 
proposal by adjusting the Historic Test Year major storm cost to include 
12 
qualifying events under this proposed definition. 
13 
 
14 
Q. 
Please explain the Company’s proposal for a reconciliation mechanism 
15 
to track minor storm costs. 
16 
A. 
Upon notification of a customer service interruption, the Company initiates 
17 
emergency response efforts to restore power as quickly as possible.  This is 
18 
an area of intense focus for the Company where continuous improvements 
19 
are consistently implemented.  In the event of a potential weather-driven 
20 
interruption, the Company prepares in advance, through active monitoring 
21 


--- Page 119 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 117 of 127 
 
of weather forecasts and even staging of crews strategically, to ensure 
1 
prompt response to any impact to service.  Further, the Company has 
2 
steadily been investing for many years to secure and harden the system.  
3 
These investments in reliability and resilience are designed to help the 
4 
system withstand challenging weather conditions and to minimize the 
5 
number of customers impacted for extended period of time when an event 
6 
does lead to interruptions.  As a result of these reactive and proactive 
7 
measures for customers, the Company has maintained a high standard of 
8 
reliability even in the face of volatile weather events and mitigated the 
9 
negative impacts of such events for our customers.  This strong customer 
10 
performance, however, has produced an increasing level of costs to respond 
11 
to weather-driven interruptions and events that do not rise to the level of a 
12 
deferrable major storm.    
13 
 
14 
Therefore, the Company proposes a mechanism to recognize the costs of 
15 
this storm performance, while at the same time protecting customers in the 
16 
event storm activity subsides and response costs materially drop from 
17 
historic levels.  Specifically, the Company proposes to implement a two-
18 
way annual reconciliation mechanism to recover the costs related to minor 
19 
storms (i.e., weather events that do not meet the major storm definition 
20 
described above), with a deadband of +/- $10 million.  To the extent that 
21 


--- Page 120 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 118 of 127 
 
annual minor storm costs exceed the established rate allowance by more 
1 
than $10 million, the Company would recover the amount that exceeds the 
2 
$10 million threshold from customers through a deferral mechanism.  If the 
3 
actual costs are below the rate allowance by more than $10 million, the 
4 
Company would defer the amount below the $10 million threshold for the 
5 
benefit of customers. 
6 
 
7 
Q.  
What are pre-staging costs and why is the Company proposing to 
8 
recover these costs? 
9 
A.  
The Company is committed to minimizing the impacts to customers even 
10 
from the most volatile weather events, consistent with the Commission’s 
11 
expectations.  To meet these expectations and mitigate weather-related 
12 
impacts to customers, the Company sometimes arranges for contract 
13 
resources to mobilize to the Company’s service territory in advance of a 
14 
predicted weather event.  This practice is referred to as “pre-staging crews.”  
15 
The costs associated with pre-staging crews are incurred regardless of 
16 
whether the weather event occurs or is as severe as predicted. 
17 
 
18 
Sometimes, weather forecasts may be severe enough to warrant pre-staging 
19 
but not result in significant interruptions of service to customers.  
20 
Nevertheless, pre-staging crews is important because the Company may not 
21 


--- Page 121 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 119 of 127 
 
otherwise be able to respond in a timely manner if the weather event does 
1 
in fact take place.   The Company does not pre-stage crews unless it appears 
2 
absolutely necessary, and the costs of these actions to protect customers  are 
3 
appropriate and should be recoverable.  Therefore, the Company proposes 
4 
to establish the deferral mechanism for recovery of pre-staging costs for 
5 
events that do not ultimately qualify as a major storm. 
6 
 
7 
Q.  
How will the Company recover its pre-staging costs? 
8 
A.  
The Company proposes that all incremental pre-staging costs for events that 
9 
qualify as major storms continue to be charged against the Major Storm 
10 
Reserve as they are today.  For those resources that are pre-staged but 
11 
ultimately are not utilized for storm restoration, and for pre-staging costs 
12 
incurred in connection with weather events that do not ultimately qualify as 
13 
a major storm, the Company proposes that all incremental pre-staging costs 
14 
(to the extent that the incremental pre-staging costs are at least $0.250 
15 
million for the event) would be charged against the Major Storm Reserve, 
16 
up to a maximum of the three largest such events per year.  Major storm 
17 
costs are shown in Exhibit __ (RRP-3), Schedule 41 and minor storm costs 
18 
are shown in Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit__RRP-3, 
19 
Schedule 2, Workpaper 2. 
20 
 
21 


--- Page 122 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel

VI. 
Performance Metrics  
15 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s electric reliability metrics. 
16 
A. 
The Company’s currently effective electric reliability metrics were set in the 
17 
2017 Niagara Mohawk Rate Case.  Specifically, there are four measures: (i) 
18 
System Average Interruption Frequency Index (“SAIFI”); (ii) Customer 
19 
Average Interruption Duration Index (“CAIDI”); (iii) Estimating; and (iv) 
20 
Inspection and Maintenance (“I&M”) Program.  Each year, the Company is 
21 


--- Page 126 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 124 of 127 
 
subject to a total pre-tax potential negative revenue adjustment of $14 
1 
million across these four metrics.  The Company is not proposing any 
2 
changes to the electric reliability metrics or associated revenue adjustment 
3 
levels in these proceedings.  Below, the Company briefly summarizes each 
4 
performance metric: 
5 
SAIFI and CAIDI 
6 
Each calendar year, if the Company’s SAIFI performance exceeds 1.08, the 
7 
Company will incur a $4 million negative revenue adjustment.  Each 
8 
calendar year, if the Company’s CAIDI performance exceeds 2.10, the 
9 
Company will incur a $4 million negative revenue adjustment. 
10 
Estimating 
11 
(a) Project Metric 
12 
In each calendar year, for each individual distribution or sub-transmission 
13 
capital project with an initial design estimate greater than $100,000, the 
14 
Company will compare the final engineering estimate of each such project 
15 
with the total actual costs for the project. The Company must achieve a 
16 
project success rate of 80 percent within plus or minus 25 percent of their 
17 
respective final engineering estimates or will be subject to a negative 
18 
revenue adjustment in the range of $1 to $3 million. 
19 
(b) Portfolio Metric 
20 


--- Page 127 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 125 of 127 
 
In each calendar year, the Company will compare the sum of all final project 
1 
actual costs against the sum of all associated final engineering estimates. If 
2 
the sum of actual project costs differs from the sum of associated project 
3 
final engineering estimates by more than plus or minus 15 percent, the 
4 
Company will be subject to a $1 million negative revenue adjustment. 
5 
 
I&M Program 
6 
Each calendar year, the Company is subject to a negative revenue 
7 
adjustment of $1 million if it fails to repair at least 85 percent of Level II 
8 
deficiencies (as defined in the Safety Orders in Case 04-M-0159 (“Safety 
9 
Orders”)) that have a repair due date in the respective calendar year within 
10 
the time period allowed for such repairs under the Safety Orders (i.e., one 
11 
year).  The Company is subject to an additional negative revenue adjustment 
12 
of $1 million if it fails to repair at least 75 percent of Level III deficiencies 
13 
(as defined in the Safety Orders) that have a repair due date in the respective 
14 
calendar year within the time period allowed for such repairs under the 
15 
Safety Orders (i.e., three years). 
16

VII. 
Research, Development and Demonstration Program 
18 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s RD&D program. 
19 
A.  
The Company’s RD&D portfolio focuses on advancing new technologies, 
20 
processes, systems, and work methods that will lead to a cleaner, more 
21 


--- Page 128 ---
Testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
 
Page 126 of 127 
 
efficient, reliable, and resilient grid.  Through its RD&D plans, the 
1 
Company seeks to (a) reduce the overall cost of delivering energy and 
2 
optimizing its system demand, (b) include safety in the design process, (c) 
3 
operate the network more efficiently by optimizing system performance, (d) 
4 
facilitate the interconnection and integration of renewable resources, and (e) 
5 
enable a sustainable design.  These goals are progressed through 
6 
collaborating with innovation partners including government agencies, 
7 
universities, technical organizations (e.g., the Electric Power Research 
8 
Institute (“EPRI”) and the Centre for Energy Advancement through 
9 
Technological Innovation (“CEATI”)), the vendor community, and industry 
10 
committees.  The Company generally leverages its RD&D investments in 
11 
organizations that collaborate research among multiple utilities, and the 
12 
Company may also seek government funding opportunities that align with 
13 
its objectives.  The Company files annually a five-year RD&D plan with 
14 
the Commission, with the most recent filing on March 31, 2020 in Matter 
15 
No. 10-00779.    
16

19 
above the Historic Test Year amount by approximately $0.16 million in the

Rate Year and approximately $0.18 million each in subsequent Data Years 
1 
1 and 2. These incremental costs are shown in Exhibit __ (EIOP-12).

Why is the Company proposing to increase cost recovery for RD&D 
4 
initiatives? 
5 
A.  
The increase in the RD&D initiatives will enable the Company to pursue 
6 
opportunities to utilize advanced technologies to meet the evolving 
7 
objectives of customers and clean energy policies.  Over the next five years, 
8 
the Company’s RD&D plan will continue to focus on the integration of 
9 
renewable resources, grid modernization, and asset management.

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program – Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  C078197 
 
Description: 
 
This project involves rebuilding the Gardenville-Dunkirk 141 (T1260) and Gardenville-
Dunkirk 142 (T1270) 115 kV transmission circuits between the Gardenville and North 
Angola Stations.  The overhead line details follow: 
 
Total length: Approximately 20 miles  
Conductor Types: Varies – 250 kcm CU, 400 kcm CU, 4/0 CU, 336 kcm ACSR, and 636 
kcm AAC, and 795 kcm ACSR.   
Number of steel structures: 250 structures (Majority of which are Ritter-Conley Flexible 
Towers with Z cross members)  
Types of structures: Double circuit, primarily steel (Z type flex), structures  
Typical Installation Date: 1930s vintage  
 
This project, also referred to as the northern phase, addresses asset condition and safety 
issues of these lines per the Overhead Line Refurbishment Strategy Paper SG080, as well 
as relieves thermal overload during periods of high power imports from Ontario and low 
loads in western NY. 
 
The specific scope for this northern section rebuild, to be completed by FY24, will 
include: 
 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 1 of 371


--- Page 152 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 2 of 371 
C003389 
Gardenville-Dunkirk 141-142 T1260-1270 
Northern Phase Rebuild 
Version 1 – 
07/22/2020 
 
 
• Rebuild both 141 and 142 lines in their entirety from the Gardenville station to the 
North Angola station with single-pole, double-circuit, davit arm steel structures. 
• Reconductor with 795 ACSR Drake. 
• Add OPGW in place of shield wire. 
• Replace transmission line switches at Lakeview switch structure. 
• Upgrade access roads (primarily in upland areas). 
• Where necessary widen ROW width to our 100’ standard for 115kV with targeted 
land purchases, easements or vegetation clearing rights.    
This project is specifically limited to the northern phase. Refurbishment of the southern 
phase from North Angola to Dunkirk (25 miles) will be addressed in a separate and 
associated project. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The primary driver for this project is asset condition per the Overhead Line 
Refurbishment Strategy SG080. The project goal is to address deteriorated assets, ensure 
the lines meet technical requirements of the NESC, and eliminate thermal overloads on 
the northern end of the lines during periods of high imports from Ontario and low load in 
western NY.  This project has received the Article VII certificate and is now in process to 
complete the EM&CP. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Rebuilding this line is necessary to provide reliable service to approximately 20,000 
customers served from eight National Grid distribution stations and a NYSEG 
distribution station. 
 
This overhead line refurbishment program promotes safety and reliability by addressing 
asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the governing National 
Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by replacing deteriorating 
structures and line components that no longer structurally or electrically conform to the 
NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
The following alternatives were also considered: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted refurbishment to extend operational life of these circuits by 15-
20 years including the replacement of only significantly deteriorated structures, replace

insulators and fittings, tower painting and footer repairs, adding optical ground wire in 
place of shield wire, and add access roads in upland areas. This alternative is not 
recommended due to the severely deteriorated condition of the steel structures. Also, 
without replacing the 4/0 Cu conductor with larger 795 ACSR Drake, loading concerns 
on the northern phase will not be addressed. 
 
Alternative 2 - System reconfiguration: This alternative is not feasible as this 
transmission line is required to serve customers. 
 
REV solutions: With thermal overloads occurring on the northern end of the 141 & 142 
lines during periods of high power imports from Ontario and low load levels in western 
NY, reducing load in the area would only exacerbate this problem. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
As the project need  is driven by asset condition, it does not meet the NWA suitability 
criteria thresholds.

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program – Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project involves the Lockport-Batavia #112 (T1510) 115 kV transmission circuit.  
The overhead line details follow: 
 
Total length: Approximately 34 miles  
Conductor Types: Varies - 250 kcm Copper 19-Strand, 795 kcm ACSR “Coot” 36/1, 
336.4 kcm ACSR “Linnet” 26/7, 428 kcm AAC 19-Strand, and 636 kcm AAC “Orchid”  
Total number of structures: 369  
Number of wood structure units: 156  
Number of steel structure units: 213  
Types of structures: Steel towers (178 of which are tri-leg towers) and wood pole 
structures (111 of which are single pole with davit arms).  
Typical Installation Date: 1930-1940’s 
 
The Lockport-Batavia #112 shares a double circuit with the Lockport-Batavia #108 for 
3.5 miles near the Batavia station. Also, for 12.6 miles beginning at the Lockport station, 
both lines run parallel with and share the Lockport-Mortimer #111 right-of-way. 
 
The budgeted scope of this life extension project includes replacement of all 178 steel tri-
leg towers and 5% of the total number of wood structures that are in deteriorated 
condition, replacement of insulators and fittings, reconductoring 17.5 miles of 428 AAC 
conductor and replacement of associated shield wire,  Relocation of 4.6 miles of the line 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 6 of 371


--- Page 157 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 7 of 371 
C003422, 
Lockport-Batavia 112, T1510 ACR 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
out of the Tonawanda Wildlife Management area and building permanent access roads in 
upland areas.   
 
The project is currently in the Develop and Sanction phase while going through the 
Article VII application process. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Based upon an engineering field evaluation, some tower and wood pole structure 
replacements are necessary along with some tower repairs due to deterioration. 
 
Conductor and shield wire testing in 2015 determined that all ACSR conductor and shield 
wire can remain in service. However, 17.5 miles of the 428 AAC conductor is being 
recommended for replacement because the calculated breaking strength was as low as 
14% below the rated breaking strength. Furthermore, this being a non-standard conductor 
it is difficult to obtain spare parts (conductor and splices) in the event of a failure. 
  
Approximately 4.6 miles of the line is located within the Tonawanda Wildlife 
Management area which is predominantly a wetland area making it very difficult for the 
Company to access for either maintenance or restoration efforts. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to provide reliable service to approximately 2,100 
customers served by Oakfield Substation. 
 
This overhead line refurbishment program promotes safety and reliability by addressing 
asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the governing National 
Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by replacing deteriorating 
structures and line components that no longer structurally or electrically conform to the 
NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
The following six (6) fit-for-purpose options to replace all steel tri-leg towers on the 
Lockport-Batavia #112 line were considered during the Option Selection (the tri-leg 
towers run between structures #6 - #211): 
 
Alternative 1 - Between Structures #6 - #175 and #188 - #211 ($31.8M): 
 
• Replace tangent structures with wood pole single circuit steel davit arm structures. 
• Replace angle and dead-end structures with steel poles on caisson foundations.

• Reroute line around the Tonawanda State Wildlife Management Area 
(“TSWMA”) between structures #142 - #160 
• Replace conductor with standard 795 kcmil 26/7 ACSR “Drake” 
• Replace shieldwire with OPGW. 
Alternative 2 - Between Structures #1 - #175 and #188 - #211 ($33.0M): 
 
• Replace tangent structures with wood pole single circuit steel davit arm structures. 
• Replace angle and dead-end structures with steel poles on caisson foundations. 
• Reroute line around the Tonawanda State Wildlife Management Area 
(“TSWMA”) between structure #142 - #160. 
• Replace conductor with standard 795 kcmil 26/7 ACSR “Drake”. 
• Replace shieldwire with OPGW. 
Alternative 3 - Between Structures #1 - #175 and #188 - #211 ($34.6M): 
 
• Replace tangent structures with wood pole equivalent single circuit steel davit 
arm structures. 
• Replace angle and dead-end structures with steel poles on caisson 
foundations. 
• Reroute line around the Tonawanda State Wildlife Management Area 
(“TSWMA”) between structure #142 - #160. 
• Replace conductor with standard 795 kcmil 26/7 ACSR “Drake”. 
• Replace shieldwire with OPGW. 
Alternative 4 - Between Structures #1 - #175 and #188 - #211 ($33.3M): 
 
• Replace conductor with standard 795 kcmil 26/7 ACSR “Drake” from 
structures #1 - #119. 
• Replace conductor with 477 ACCR “Hawk” conductor, which has equivalent 
ampacity as the standard 795 kcmil 26/7 ACSR “Drake”, from structures #119 
- #175 and #188 - #211. 
• Replace shieldwire with OPGW. 
• Remove all tangent structures. 
• Install new wood pole equivalent single circuit steel davit arm structures 
structures with increased span lengths resulting in approximately 25% 
reduction in overall suspension structures within the 8 mile section of the line 
beginning at structure #119.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  C073999, C076185 
 
Description: 
 
The project scope includes the asset separation/replacement at Dunkirk Substation.  The 
asset separation will include a new control house and equipment on the existing land 
within Dunkirk substation to allow for National Grid owned equipment within the NRG 
owned Dunkirk power plant to be removed.  The NRG Dunkirk power plant was 
mothballed on January 1, 2016.     
 
There will be assets throughout the National Grid substation at the 230kV, 115kV and 
34.5kV that are going to be replaced to maintain system reliability. The 230kV and 
115kV assets will be replaced one for one per the asset condition issues.  The 34.5V 
assets are planned for replacement with a metal-clad switchgear to efficiently cutover due 
to limited working space. 
 
A series 115kV tie-circuit breaker scheme is to be installed to support transmission 
system reliability. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The National Grid owned Dunkirk substation interconnects with the NRG owned 
Dunkirk Power Plant.  The substation serves as an interconnection to the electrical grid at 
the 230, 115 and 34.5kV levels.  The plant was originally constructed in the early 1950s 
by Niagara Mohawk as the owner of generation, transmission and sub-transmission

          Page 13 of 371

C005155 
Dunkirk - Rebuild 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
assets. National Grid’s major equipment includes four transformers: two (2) new 
230/120/13.2kV 125MVA autotransformers and two (2) 115/34.5kV 41.7MVA 
transformers supplying four (4) 230kV transmission lines, five (5) 115kV transmission 
lines and two (2) 34.5kV sub-transmission lines as well as NRG’s station service.  
 
National Grid retains ownership of most of the 230kV, 115kV, and 34.5kV switch yard; 
however, the controls are located in the generation control room owned by NRG. 
 
There are asset condition issues at the Dunkirk substation.  The foundations are in poor 
condition in the 230kV and 34.5kV yards affecting the integrity of the structures. Some 
circuit breaker foundations are in very poor condition raising the possibility that an oil 
circuit breaker (OCB) could move during a severe fault leading to more damage and/or 
causing safety issues. 
 
The five (5) 230kV OCBs are Westinghouse type GW design (1958 through 1961) and 
would be part of the OCB replacement program, if not for this project.  The 230kV 
Westinghouse Type O bushings are a concern as the power factor and capacitance results 
are trending upwards. 
 
The 230/120/13.2kV autotransformers differential relaying is in need of upgrading to 
address inadequate protection (presently there is no tertiary differential).  The 230kV, 
115kV and 34.5kV disconnects have become problematic from an operational standpoint.   
 
The 230kV bushing potential devices (BPDs) have become problematic due to poor 
condition and the remaining BPDs will likely have to be replaced in the near future. 
Fencing around the yard is not compliant with National Grid standards and requires 
repair at the base or a berm built up to restrict animal entrance. 
 
The conduit system carrying control wires has degraded to the point that the integrity of 
the control wires has been compromised.  Control wires inside the plant have also seen 
insulation degradation. In some cases, the wiring is so poor that troubleshooting abilities 
are limited for fear of handling control wires with degraded insulation.  Grounds, alarms 
or breaker mis-operations happen more frequently during periods of heavy rain, 
indicating poor insulation below ground. 
 
National Grid has recently replaced both 230-120-13.2kV 125MVA GE autotransformers 
with new ABB 230-120-13.2kV 125MVA autotransformers and all 115kV OCBs with 
new SF6 breakers, foundations and control cable. 
 
The plant was originally constructed with generation, transmission and sub-transmission 
assets combined, including station service, battery, relaying, alarm/annunciation, control 
and communications.  All troubleshooting, maintenance testing, equipment replacement 
and upgrades require excellent knowledge of the plant operation. NRG and National Grid

must maintain good lines of communication and share updated prints to preserve

There are parallel efforts underway to address these issues.  In the short term, a project 
was approved to install a new cable trench in the 230kV yard in 2009 and was completed 
in the summer of 2010. Control cables deemed faulty can be replaced using these new 
facilities.  Conceptual engineering has been completed for a new control house and

Customer Benefit: 
 
The planned replacement of this substation reduces the likelihood of an in-service failure 
which can lead to long-term interruptions of the transmission system as well as customer 
outages. It also serves to separate the assets between National Grid and NRG. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Do Nothing: This was rejected since the existing substation is a shared facility with NRG 
and would not allow for asset separation.  Also, leaving the equipment this way would 
create additional maintenance issues and allow for the possibility of a larger spread 
resulting from a fault.

As the project need is now and it is driven by asset condition, it does not meet the NWA

Program Name:  
Wood Pole Management 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
The wood pole management program includes the replacement of deteriorated wood 
poles identified by Osmose Utilities (“Osmose”) during ground line inspections as being 
a ‘Reject’, ‘Priority Reject’, or ‘Restorable Reject’ (a Restorable Reject is a wood pole 
that is eligible for external reinforcement to restore its ground-line strength).  The annual 
ground line inspections cover approximately 10% of the Company’s transmission wood 
poles and where the remaining residual pole strength is calculated taking into account the 
presence of internal and external decay and provides additional treatment and insecticide 
if required.   
 
This wood pole management program is in addition to the Company’s Inspection and 
Maintenance program’s (“I&M”, C026923) five-year foot patrol which is required under 
the Commission’s 2005 Safety Order in Case 04-M-0159. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
This program replaces deteriorated wood poles and structures, as needed, that no longer 
meet National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) requirements.     
 
A wood pole identified as a “Reject” fails to meet code requirements for extreme design 
conditions when the pole has two-thirds, or less, of its original design strength.  Priority 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 18 of 371

Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 19 of 371 
C011640 
Wood Pole Management Program 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Reject poles are those that fall below one-third of its original design strength and 
potentially can fail under conditions considered to be “normal” circumstances. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The wood pole management program promotes safety and reliability by replacing Reject 
and Priority Reject wood structures that no longer structurally or electrically conform to 
the NESC before they fail in service. 
 
Storm resiliency during severe weather events is the greatest concern for Reject poles and 
structures. Failures can hamper service restoration efforts, increase outage durations and 
raise public safety concerns. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Only replace visual rotting wood structures in the I&M program, when a 
line is refurbished, or as pole failures occur:  While the I&M program will identify 
deteriorated poles based on ‘pole sounding’ techniques, this program provides a more 
qualitative means of identifying deteriorated poles that may not be captured during 
sounding. 
 
Alternative 2 - REV solutions: Cannot be implemented as these assets are still necessary 
to support the transmission system. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative:   
 
Due to this project being driven by Asset Condition, it does not meet the NWA 
Suitability Criteria.

TLine I&M Program: E014130 
 
Description: 
 
The goal of this program is to replace deteriorated, damaged or failed components on the 
transmission overhead line system identified during five-year foot patrol inspections.  
This follows standard industry practice and the Commission’s 2005 Safety Order in Case 
04-M-0159. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The primary driver of this project is to meet the Company’s regulatory obligations under 
the 2005 Safety Order.  In addition, performing identified maintenance and capital repair 
work will benefit customers by enhancing the safety and reliability of transmission line 
assets and maintain the structural integrity of lines. 
 
The project scope is limited to replacing assets identified from the inspection of 
transmission line assets specifically obtained by a) foot patrol visual inspections, b)

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program – Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
 The scope of work for this project includes the rebuild of the southern portion of the 
#151, #152, and #167 circuits (37.4 miles). Conductor work of the line will begin at 
structure 199, while structure work will begin at structure 200 in Concord, NY and 
continue to the Five Mile Rd Substation in Humphrey, NY.  
 
This portion of the line primarily consists of double circuit steel flex towers, steel square 
base lattice towers, and wood two pole suspension structures. There are a total of 364 
structures in the southern portion of the circuit. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
This line was originally built in the 1920’s. However, it was rebuilt from the Gardenville 
Substation to structure 199 in 2011. Due to the age and condition of the southern portion 
of the lines, which includes structure 200 to the Five Mile Rd Substation, National Grid 
has determined that this portion of the line will be rebuilt.  
 
The 151/152/167 was first identified approximately 15 years ago as a candidate by 
Transmission Line Engineering for refurbishment based on asset condition at that time. 
Since then, vangs have failed, the steel has not been painted, and the circuit has been re-
Exhibit___(EIOP-6)

Gard-HH 151-152 T1950-T1280 S ACR 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
inspected to re-confirm its asset condition.  
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The benefit for this ACR is reliability and safety. There are numerous National Grid 
substations, a NYSEG substation, switching stations, and municipal substations served by 
these circuits. There are 4,244 radial customers served by the 158 circuit which is 
supplied by the 152/167. In addition, Machias has 1,557 customers.  
 
Reconductoring with a larger conductor will provide more resilience in the transmission 
system over the current 336 30/7 ACSR and will match the current northern phase 
ampacity. In addition, it will relieve the congestion shown in the NYISO 2019 
Congestion Assessment and Resource Integration Study (CARIS) 70 x 30 scenario and 
enable additional renewable energy to reach the market.   
 
An additional benefit is improved Public Safety by hardening critical crossings.  
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Refurbishment (Preferred Option) 
 
For this Option, the existing steel towers will be inspected and remain in service if 
deemed in good condition. Insulator vangs, insulators, and hardware will all be replaced. 
The two shield wires in this option would be replaced with the standard steel.  
 
Alternative 2 - Refurbishment w/ Steel & 795 ACSR  
 
For this Option, the existing assets would be replaced with a combination of steel poles 
on concrete foundations for the dead-ends and direct-embedded steel poles with steel 
davit arms for the tangents. The conductor would be replaced with 795 ACSR Drake. 
One of the two shield wires in this option would be replaced with OPGW the other would 
be replaced with the standard steel.  
 
Alternative 3 - Refurbishment w/ Steel & 477 ACCR  
 
For this Option, the existing assets would be replaced with a combination of steel poles 
on concrete foundations for the dead-ends and direct-embedded steel poles with steel 
davit arms for the tangents. The conductor would be replaced with 477 ACCR Hawk. 
One of the two shield wires in this option would be replaced with OPGW the other would 
be replaced with the standard steel.

Description: 
 
This project will address asset condition related issues on the 115kV Mountain to 
Lockport 103 (T1620) and Mountain to Lockport 104 (T1060).  
 
These two circuits are primarily run on joint steel lattice structures. The overhead line 
details follow: 
 
Total length: 17.59 miles (T1620) / 17.63 Miles (T1060) 
Conductor Types: 795 Al 37 Str. / 636 Al 37 Str. / 400 CU 19 Str. 
Total number of structures: 238 
Total Steel: 178 
Total Wood: 60 
Types of structures: Flex Lattice, Square Lattice, Steel Davit, Wood H-Frame, Wood 
Davit Arm, Wood Other. 
Installation Date: 1922 (oldest record in Power plant) 
Conductor Clearance: Completed on both circuits 
 
This project will target the replacement of the remaining brown porcelain insulators 
which are in deteriorated condition. As part of this project, the steel shield wire will also 
be harvested and tested for rated breaking strength. Towers and poles will also be 
inspected, and replaced if needed.

Project Justification: 
 
The 17.6 mile line is of 1920s vintage and is in need of refurbishment. The circuit is still 
using deteriorating brown porcelain insulators which need to be replaced.  
 
The 103/104 lines have 11,599 and 6,326 (respectively) customers at risk. The 103 line 
has experienced eight (8) outages since 2014. Furthermore, the 104 line has experienced 
13 outages since 2014. The replacement of the deteriorated insulators will aim to reduce 
the number of outages for customers. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to provide reliable service to customers served by 
National Grid.  This overhead line refurbishment program promotes safety and reliability 
by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the 
governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by 
replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Refurbishment 
 
In this Option:  
 
• Structures deemed Reject would be replaced  
• All insulators and hardware would be replaced with toughened glass  
• Conductor will be evaluated and remain in service if passed 
• Shield wire would be evaluated and remain in service if passed 
Alternative 2 - Targeted Insulator Replacements (Preferred Option) 
 
In this Option:  
 
• Deteriorated brown porcelain insulators between structure 61 and structure 86 will 
be replaced with toughened glass (27 structures).  
• 
These deteriorated insulators were left "stranded" in between sections of new 
insulators that have been installed as part of various projects over recent years.

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program – Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
The scope of work for this project includes refurbishment of the Niagara/Packard-
Gardenville 180/182 circuits.  The existing steel towers will be inspected and remain in 
service if deemed in good condition. Insulator vangs, insulators, and hardware will all be 
replaced. In addition, the two shield wires will be replaced with the standard steel shield 
wires. 
 
The Niagara-Gardenville #180 extends 31.7 miles and contains approximately 171 
towers. The Packard-Gardenville #182 extends 29.3 miles and contains 284 towers 
(Including 1 mile of tap). 
 
Project Justification: 
 
This line was originally built in the 1920’s. Due to the age and condition of these lines, 
National Grid has indicated that the 180/182 circuits should be refurbished. Typical 
towers on these circuits are square base lattice and lattice flex towers. 
 
The 180/182 lines have a history of poor performance with multiple interruptions in the 
recent years. Niagara-Gardenville #180 has experienced 16 interruptions from 1/15/2013 
to 6/7/2019. The Packard-Gardenville #182 has experienced 19 interruptions from 
2/21/2013 to 6/7/2019.

The Niagara-Gardenville #180 serves 3,857 customers and the Packard-Gardenville #182

Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Refurbishment (Preferred Option) 
 
For this Option, the existing steel towers will be inspected and remain in service if 
deemed in good condition. Insulator vangs, insulators, and hardware will all be replaced. 
The two shield wires in this option would be replaced with the standard steel.  
 
Alternative 2 - Reconductoring on Existing Towers w/Hybrid Conductor 
 
For this Option, the existing steel towers will be inspected and remain in service if 
deemed in good condition. Insulator vangs, insulators, and hardware will all be replaced. 
The two shield wires in this option would be replaced with the standard steel. The 
existing conductor will be replaced with a hybrid on the same towers. 
 
Alternative 3 - Refurbishment w/ Steel & 795 ACSR 
 
For this Option, the existing assets would be replaced with a combination of steel poles 
on concrete foundations for the dead-ends and direct-embedded steel poles with steel 
davit arms for the tangents. The conductor would be replaced with 795 ACSR Drake. 
One of the two shield wires in this option would be replaced with OPGW the other would 
be replaced with the standard steel.

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program – Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  None 
 
Description: 
 
This project involves the Pannell-Geneva 4-4A (T1860) 115 kV “bussed” transmission 
circuits.   
 
Total length: Approximately 25 miles 
Conductor Types: 795 kcm ACSR “Coot” and 336.4 kcm ACSR “Oriole” 
Number of wood structure units: 8 
Number of steel structure units: 265 
Types of structures: steel lattice towers, Blaw Knox dead-end towers, wood pole 
structures, flex towers, and steel pole. 
Estimate Installation Date: 1900 to 1920’s 
 
The scope of this project is to reinforce the sections of line that cross critical areas such 
as roads, railroads and water. To do this, the preferred option is to replace conductor, 
insulators and hardware over critical the crossings.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
This line is necessary to provide reliable 115kV network service to RG&E and 
NYSE&G. National Grid owns this line connecting RG&E’s Pannell station and 
NYSE&G’s Border City (Geneva) station.
