Line Core conductor testing on the neighboring Mortimer-Pannell 24 115kV line, which 
is the same vintage and conductor type as this Pannell-Geneva 4-4A lines, shows Zinc 
loss due to corrosion.  
 
There are known asset condition issues on the line including conductor failures as 
recently as January 2020 with associated safety concerns. Since 2014, the 4/4A line has 
experienced (26) outages. Of these (26) outages, (7) are directly confirmed as a conductor 
issue. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to support the 115kV transmission network.  
 
This project, part of the Overhead Line Refurbishment program, promotes safety and 
reliability by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to 
meet the governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built 
by replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Address (14) Crossings that are County Road or above in significance 
• Replace (18) towers with Dead-end DE Steel Poles w/ guy wires 
• Replace both circuits of conductor totaling 7700 corridor feet 
• Install Smart Fault indicators at crossings 
 
Alternative 2 - Reconductoring this circuit using 795 ACSR: This option would convert 
the line into a single circuit instead of a bused circuit, however it may require 100% 
structure replacement if it is determined the existing structures cannot support the weight 
of the 795 ACSR.  
 
Alternative 3 - Reconductoring this circuit using an alternate conductor type: This will 
consider lighter conductors to try and salvage the existing towers. 
 
Alternative 4 - Rebuilding the circuit with wood poles: If the structures are not able to be 
reused and must be replaced, single-circuit wood pole structures will be considered. 
  
Alternative 5 - System reconfiguration: This alternative is not feasible as this 
transmission line is required to connect RG&E and NYSE&G stations. 
 
Alternative 6 - REV solutions: Cannot be implemented as these assets are still necessary

Program Name:

Associated Funding Numbers: C073996, C073997, C074342, C074322 
 
Description: 
 
This project builds a new Lighthouse Hill substation is  at a greenfield location 
approximately 1.5 miles away from the existing substation location..  The new substation 
will be comprised of a 115kV transmission switching substation with a breaker-and-a-
half design, 115-34.5kV substation, and 115-12kV distribution substation. This will also 
require transmission, sub transmission, and distribution line relocations from the current 
substation to the new site approximately a half mile away. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The 115kV, 34.5kV and 12kV assets at Lighthouse Hill Substation are in deteriorated 
condition, history of leaks from the Oil filled equipment, mechanism issues, limited spare 
parts, limited to no Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support, broken insulators 
and disconnects. The new site also eliminates the flood risk potential and provides 
separation of National Grid assets from the Brookfield owned power house. There are six 
(6) 115kV Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs) in total at the substation. There are five (5) that 
are part of the NY OCB replacement strategy and manufactured by General Electric with 
one (1) in 1956 and four (4) in 1962. The remaining the OCB was manufactured by 
Federal Pacific in 1956 and has indicated the same type history as the General Electric 
OCBs which is deterioration, no spare parts, no OEM support and mechanism issues.

There are two (2) units A and B that are paralleled to make Transformer #6 which is a

mechanism issues, oil leaks, no spare parts and no OEM support. 
 
There are two (2) 12kV grounding transformers at the substation that were manufactured 
by General Electric in 1983.  The grounding transformers have deteriorated over their

There is one (1) 34.5kV oil circuit breaker manufactured by General Electric in 1956 and

There are two (2) 12kV circuit breakers that have had a history of mechanism issues, no 
spare parts and no OEM support. They are oil circuit breaker R455 which was

which was manufactured by Yin Electric Company in 1981.

the 115kV S&C circuit switcher Mark II, and the sixty-three (63) cap and pin insulators.

pertain to our assets in the substation yard.  These assets are obsolete, do not have spare

replaced due to projects and/or damage failure.

system as well as customer outages.

the 34.5kV and 12kV are straight bus designs.  The 34.5kV transformation can be 
connected to a bus, but the 12kV transformation is to be interconnected to the breaker and

Program Name:  
Substation Batteries 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
Substation Batteries and Chargers are one of the more crucial assets within a Substation. 
These batteries provide backup power to the relays that operation equipment in the yard 
and communication equipment upon loss of power to the control house. This program is 
for the purchase and replacement of substation batteries and chargers in the Company's 
Upstate NY operating territories due primarily to asset condition issues. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The primary driver for this program is asset condition of battery and charger systems 
which are critical components of a substation and required to ensure full operational 
capability during both normal and abnormal system conditions in substations. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
By proactively replacing substation batteries and chargers the Company is able to 
maintain safe operating conditions for both Company personnel and customers. This 
allows for restoration activities to be executed during system contingencies, mitigating 
the amount of time needed to restore power to customers.

Description: 
 
This project is to replace the 115kV assets with a 115kV open air breaker and a half 
substation, reconnect the transmission lines and the two (2) 115kV – 13.2kV power 
transformers, and install a second capacitor bank. The installation of a new control house 
for the 115k protection and control equipment and these will be tied back in with the 
15kV assets. 
 
The replacement of the 115kV assets maintains the reliability of the system by replacing 
assets in poor condition.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
The 115kV portion of Oneida substation has Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs), pin and cap 
insulators, disconnects that all have had a history of asset condition issues.    
 
There are five (5) 115kV Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs) that are large OCBs and have had 
a history of leaks, mechanism issues, lack spare parts and have no/limited Original 
Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support.  There is a mixture of OCB manufacturers of 
General Electric, Westinghouse, and Federal Pacific from 1959 to 1962.  There are two 
(2) OCBs manufactured by General Electric type FK and one (1) manufactured by 
Westinghouse type BZO that have a family issue identified in the NY OCB replacement

The remaining 115kV asset concerns within the station are the nineteen (19) manual

The substation has 115kV vertical bus as compared to horizontal bus which is a safety

The substation has seven (7) 115kV transmission lines that are part of the central to east

non-IEC-61850 pertaining to the protection, controls and telecommunication assets. 
 
The Oneida Substation also has a 115kV-13.2kV portion with straight bus design, with 
vertical busses. The 115kV-13.2kV transformers and 13.2kV portion of the yard were 
replaced in 2014.  
 
The existing control house was renovated as part the 2014 project and presently has room 
to install the new relay and controls for the 115kV project.

Program Name:

Associated Funding Numbers:  C073991 
 
Description: 
 
The project scope includes the asset replacement of the 115kV and 12kV equipment at 
Lockport Substation.  The assets will include Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs), disconnect 
switches, potential transformers, a power transformer, steel structures, and foundations.  
 
A new control house will be installed to ensure a suitable location is created to keep the 
relays and communication equipment protected.     
 
Project Justification: 
 
Lockport substation was originally part of the 25 cycle system dating back to the 1910’s 
and is currently a major 115kV transmission substation with thirteen (13) 115kV 
transmission lines connected through the East and West bus sections.  The overall 
condition of the station yard and control room is poor.  Work is required on control cable 
duct banks, breaker operators, structure painting and concrete equipment foundations that 
are deteriorated significantly.  
 
The original manhole and duct system for control cables is in degraded condition which 
has caused control wire shorts, battery grounds and unwanted circuit breaker operations. 
Station maintenance crews are restricted in performing repairs due to the overall 
condition of the duct bank because single control cables cannot be replaced without

Lockport - Asset Replacements

adversely affecting adjacent control cables in the same ducts. 
 
There are four forty-year old 115kV oil filled BZ0 breakers which have been identified in 
the New York OCB strategy for replacement. 
 
Transformer #60 is a 115-12kV 7.5MVA transformer manufactured in 1941 which 
supplies Lockport’s station service and Race Street Line 751 which is tied to the Race 
Street seasonal hydraulic unit.  An alternate station service should be provided should TR 
#60 or station service fail. 
 
The control room building is also in very poor condition and requires replacement. It is 
an oversized building with continued maintenance costs for the original roof and the 
intricate brickwork. It contains a 90 ton overhead crane in the old 25 cycle frequency 
changer portion of the building which is presently used only to store old cable.  The 
control house roof was repaired in the 1990s and brick pointing was also done to limit 
deterioration within the last 5 years. The old 25 cycle control circuitry has been 
disconnected with the DC battery to eliminate potential source of battery ground 
problems.   
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The planned replacement of the substation assets reduces the likelihood of an in-service 
failure due to deteriorated assets which can lead to long-term interruptions of the 
transmission system as well as customer outages. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Lockport – Asset Replacement 
The replacement of the 115kV OCBs, 115kV-12kV power transformer, 12kV assets that 
support the generation to National Grid connection, and the construction of a new control 
house.  
 
Alternative 2 - Lockport – Asset Replacement as a Breaker and a Half layout 
The replacement of the 115kV OCBs, 115kV-12kV power transformer, 12kV assets that 
support the generation to National Grid connection, and the construction of a new control 
house.  
 
Alternative 3 -Lockport – Asset Replacement as a Gas Insulated Substation (GIS) 
The replacement of the 115kV OCBs, 115kV-12kV power transformer, 12kV assets that 
support the generation to National Grid connection, and the construction of a new control 
house.

Program Name:

Description: 
 
This project will address remaining asset condition issues on the Ticonderoga-Whitehall 
#3 T5830 and Ticonderoga-Republic #2 T5810 115kV transmission lines.  The following 
are details regarding the circuit: 
 
Total length: Approximately 42.2 miles total with approximately 19.7 miles on the T5810 
and 22.5 miles on the T5830  
Conductor Types: Ticonderoga-Republic 2: 336.4 kcmil ACSR 30/7 “Oriole” and 4/0 7-
strand BSCU conductors.  OHGW 1-7/16” EHS CW and 1-3/8” HS CW. Ticonderoga-
Whitehall 3: 336.4 kcmil ACSR 30/7 “Oriole” conductor.  OHGW: 1-7/16” EHS CW 
Total number of structures: 350 
Number of wood structure units: 343 (original poles were Western Red Cedar) 
Number of steel structure units: 7  
Types of structures: Single circuit, primarily consisting of wood pole H-frame structures 
and steel lattice towers  
Typical Installation Date: 1920-1930s 
Last Osmose Inspection: 2016 
Conductor Clearance: To be completed concurrently with ACR 
 
The project scope for this refurbishment project includes:

Project Justification: 
 
The line was evaluated using the following resources to determine its component 
properties and develop the project scope: 
 
• Wood pole ground line evaluation was performed by Osmose in 2016.  Osmose 
performed pole inspection and treatment on all wood poles.  As part of the 
Osmose inspection it was determined whether the wood pole requires replacement 
based on an external and internal investigation. 
• Aerial oblique photos were taken during the summer of 2016.  The oblique 
photographs were used to visually evaluate the wood pole tops for decay, 
woodpecker activity, hardware issues, and overall general condition at the top of 
the poles. 
• In 2016 a steel structure footer contractor evaluated and refurbished the legs on all 
seven (7) of the steel structures. 
• Coupons, i.e. steel samples, from the ACSR and BSCU conductor and overhead 
ground wire were lab tested to determine their existing tensile strength, 
brittleness, and the amount of residual zinc on the steel core within the ACSR is 
remaining. 
• An aerial comprehensive inspection was completed in FY18 to evaluate the 
connections and hardware on the seven (7) steel towers.

Alternatives:

determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Due to the 
timing of the need, it was determined that this project will not be evaluated for a potential 
NWA.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project removes the 4/0 copper in service on both circuits by reconductoring and 
rebuilding a significant portion of line #3 and all of line #10. Presently, lines #3 and #10 
are co-located over a distance of approximately 13.1 miles before line #3 departs the 
shared right-of-way, eventually connecting to the DeWitt Substation.  This project is 
presently under construction. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
During the 2011 Central Division Area Study, the Clay – Teall #10 and Clay – Dewitt #3 
lines were identified as being over their acceptable loading during contingencies 
including multi-element single contingencies (stuck-breaker contingency) and multiple 
outage contingencies (two parallel lines, one after another). At the time of that study 
operational measures were identified and implemented to mitigate concerns with the 
single contingency issues – specifically, Bartell Road substation was moved to its 
alternate tap feed to reduce line loading on Clay – Teall #10, which was the heavier 
loaded line. This resulted in reduced post-contingency loading on the line and meant that 
all remaining issues were for N-1-1 (multiple element) contingencies. Additionally, this 
mitigation prevented either line from exceeding its short term emergency (STE) rating 
under contingency in the 2012 and 2016 case years. It was not until the 2021 case year 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 64 of 371


--- Page 215 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 65 of 371 
C043995 
Clay-Teall#10, Clay-Dewitt#3 
Reconductoring 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
(under projected load growth assumed in the study) that the STE ratings would be 
exceeded. 
 
Further analysis of operational mitigation identified a number of short-term solutions that 
would be acceptable until such time as a permanent solution could be put in place. The 
permanent solutions were determined, and projects were initiated. 
 
In subsequent years of analysis of the Central Division system conditions had changed – 
including, but not limited, to the retirement of generation in the Syracuse and surrounding 
areas as well as changing patterns of flow through the system related to transfers between 
parts of the State. These changes have resulted in higher flows than previously identified 
in the initial study and have driven the need for the permanent solutions to be 
implemented. All of the analysis performed in the 2011 study was done with the best 
information available at the time which identified a need but did not trigger a necessity to 
expedite work. As system conditions have changed in the past few years this work has 
become more critical for the reliability of the area. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Reconductoring the limiting elements of the line will eliminate operational actions 
currently being used to mitigate contingency limits. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Re-routing lines alternative: Various line “re-configurations” were 
considered that would meet the capacity requirements and still serve existing 
substations/load.  This alternative was dismissed due to greater system and environmental 
impacts. 
 
Alternative 2 - Underground 115kV line alternative: An underground routing alternative 
that followed the existing line corridor was considered along with two “dips” scenarios; 
where the line is placed underground for short lengths.  While the path that follows the 
existing ROW meets the primary electrical requirements, the existing ROW crosses over 
several roadways, established wetlands, wetland buffer zones, and other sensitive 
resource areas.  Additionally, cost to install the underground 115kV transmission lines 
historically are six to ten times more costly than overhead construction.

Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Load relief upgrades directly increase the maximum hosting capacity of the local EPS 
(electric power system) by two mechanisms. Increased asset capacity allows for a higher 
reverse power flow. Additionally, it allows more load to interconnect, which generally 
increases the threshold for certain higher cost interconnection upgrades (such as 3V0). 
This will enable PV and ESS to interconnect at higher volumes with a lower marginal 
interconnection cost. VVO directly contributes to system efficiency, contributing to EE 
targets, as well as reducing energy required from carbon heavy generation (by reducing 
the total energy procured from NYISO). Increasing efficiency also reduces peak loading, 
which may decrease the need for 'dirty' peaker plants. Transmission upgrades will 
eliminate congestions and allow for a more lower cost clean energy to reach load centers.

Description: 
 
Royal Ave Substation (C044594 and C044874): This project will construct a new, 
standard 115-13.2kV / 40MVA two transformer substation using metal-clad switchgear 
on National Grid property located north of the existing substation site.  The secondary 
bus tie breaker will be operated as normally open.   Feeder reactors will be installed to 
maintain the fault duty at the indoor substation within acceptable values.  Installation of 
new equipment will occur on the adjacent lands such that the existing substation can 
remain in service during the construction of the new station.  Upon completion of the 
installation, this project will begin to cutover new distribution 13.2kV feeders to the new 
equipment and will remove all of the existing outdoor electrical equipment.   The 
transmission service connection will be relocated and will remain as a dual-tap 
configuration from the existing Dupont – Packard #183 & #184 115kV lines.

will house both the incoming 13.2kV breakers for high-side bank protection as well as 
the 4.8kV feeder breakers for feeder protection.  Installation of new equipment will occur

Project Justification: 
 
Asset condition is the primary driver on this project.  Due to the high energy electrical 
discharge present in the Harper transformers and its failure history, plus the amount of 
overdutied equipment at the outdoor substations and their failure history, it is 
recommended to also install new outdoor substations and utilize adjacent land owned by 
the company. 
    
Replacement of the substations as recommended in this project is consistent with 
National Grid's goal of improving safety and reliability for the following reasons: 
 
• Due to the design and condition of these substations, there is a higher probability 
than normal for a human factors event.  In addition, the condition of these 
substations creates a higher probability than normal for a failure to occur. 
 
• Since control, protection, cabling, circuit breakers, and structure are obsolete; a 
failure of a single component in the substation may not be easily fixed. This 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6)

situation will cause an extended outage and in many cases the component will 
have to be replaced. 
• Most of the replacements covered by this project are at locations where there is a 
significant and immediate reliability risk should a failure occur.  Under normal 
conditions, failure of a component could result in immediate and sustained 
customer outage until some type of a replacement is installed. 
• Failure to replace these substations leaves National Grid open to the exposures 
identified above.  At all indoor substations, a simple equipment failure could have 
a significant reliability impact. 
• Executing this project will also improve operations by removing aging assets 
from at risk locations. 
• This project addresses Asset Management’s goals by removing obsolete, aging 
and problematic assets from the system.  
• Circuit outage availability is very limited. Unplanned outages can cause 
significant disruption to planned work and impact the availability and reliability 
of the distribution system and customers. Indoor substation equipment failures 
can result in increased loading on parallel units which may increase the risk of 
multiple failures. 
Customer Benefit: 
 
This recommended project includes the replacement of existing equipment with new and 
upgraded equipment and will deliver improved substations with all safety, operational 
and maintenance issues resolved.  It also mitigates risks to reliability with an extended 
outage due to equipment failure.  The recommended plan provides capacity to support 
economic development in the town of Niagara Falls and sets the stage for future 
infrastructure development for the area.  
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - An indoor substation refurbishment similar to the Buffalo substation 
rebuilds:  This also includes the installation of a New Harper substation; however, it was 
decided it unnecessary to keep and maintain the existing buildings.  In addition, there is 
also enough space within the substation footprints to build new equipment without being 
in close proximity to energized equipment.   Utilizing recent investment grade estimates 
from “Buffalo Style” substation rebuilds and the conceptual report for Harper substation. 
 
Alternative 2 - An indoor substation refurbishment by utilizing padmount distribution 
class equipment: This also includes the installation of a New Harper substation.  The 
distribution class equipment does not conform to the Company’s substation standards,

considered a distribution center instead of a substation.  As such, some level of risk in 
terms of schedule and cost would be assumed due to the non-standard nature of this 
equipment.   
 
Alternative 3 - An indoor substation refurbishment by retiring existing assets at Eighth 
Street #80, Welch Avenue #83 and Stephenson Avenue #85:  This also includes the 
installation of a New Harper substation.  This would require the voltage conversion of 
existing 4kV loads to 13.2kV.  However, due to the boundaries mentioned in the 
background section and the added costs/time to rebuild and convert feeder mainlines to 
13.2kV this option was rejected.  In addition, lessons learned with efforts to rebuild the 
City of Niagara Falls to 13.2 kV from 4.16 kV and 4.8 kV in the 1990’s indicate that it is 
a very slow and expensive process.  Rebuilding the substations is more effective to deal 
with asset replacement issues in a timely fashion.  This option is estimated at 
approximately $38M. 
 
Alternative 4 - An indoor substation refurbishment by replacing Harper substation and 
installing two (2) new Modular Integrated Transportable Substations (MITS) on property 
located within the existing Welch Avenue and Stephenson Avenue substation fences:  
The two MITS units would be broken into two separate skids, one for the high side 
protection and transformer and another for the regulators and reclosers.  Installation of 
new equipment would occur on the adjacent station property such that the station can 
remain in service during the new construction phase.  This alternative was hampered by a 
lack of vendor information to adequately determine if equipment may be protected.   In 
addition, the MITS scheme is not capable of supporting a secondary bus tie.  If a bus tie 
is added, a low side interrupting device would be required.  Also, MITS units are better 
suited for applications involving a single bus section and fewer feeders such as the case 
with Eighth Street Substation #80.  Due to the above concerns this option is not 
recommended and due to the protection issues mentioned no estimate is provided. 
 
Alternative 5 - Substation refurbishment project similar to the preferred alternative but 
operates all of the substations with a normally open secondary bus tie scheme:   This 
alternative does not require the use of feeder reactors at Harper Station. The arc flash 
analysis and mitigation program requires that estimates of the maximum available heat 
energy to which employees could be exposed to shall be determined and that control 
methods shall be implemented to mitigate exposure. With the implementation of a 
normally open secondary bus tie scheme, and the installation of feeder reactors at Harper, 
the maximum available heat energy to which employees are exposed to will be within 8 
cal/cm^2.   This option is estimated at approximately $24.1M. 
 
Alternative 6 - Defer or do nothing: This is not recommended because these concerns 
represent risk to National Grid assets, reliability, safety and customer service.

Description: 
 
This project involves the Mortimer-Pannell 24 25 115 kV transmission lines.   
 
Total length: Approximately 15.7 miles 
Conductor Types: 336.4 kcm ACSR “Oriole” 
Number of wood structure units: 78 
Number of steel structure units: 172 
Types of structures: steel lattice towers, Blaw Knox dead-end towers, wood pole 
structures, flex towers. 
Estimated Installation Date: 1907 and 1940’s 
 
The  scope for this project is for the  conductor replacement  the entire length of the lines.   
due to recent Line Core conductor testing results of the Mortimer-Pannell 24 115kV line 
showing Zinc loss due to corrosion.   Shield wire will be installed the entire length of the 
lines. Installing permanent access roads to upland areas is also included. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Line Core conductor testing results of the Mortimer-Pannell 24 115kV line show Zinc

loss due to corrosion.  Transmission Planning has also identified capacity concerns with 
these circuits.   
 
There are known asset condition issues on the line and over eighty (80) incidents reported 
in IDS since 1990, most of which are during summer months leading to the conclusion 
the lack of shield wire and insufficient grounding on the line leaves it vulnerable to 
lightning strikes.  
 
These circuits are is necessary to provide a reliable 115kV network from Rochester Gas 
& Electric (RGE) Pannell station.  Pannell station is a source to the 115kV network. And 
these lines are a key west-east component of the system. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to support the 115kV transmission network.  
 
This project, part of the Overhead Line Refurbishment program, promotes safety and 
reliability by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to 
meet the governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built 
by replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Reconductoring this circuit using 795 kcm ACSR: This option may 
require 100% structure replacement if it is determined the existing structures cannot 
support the weight of the 795 kcm ACSR. 
  
Alternative 2 - Reconductoring this circuit using an alternate conductor type: If 
reconductoring is necessary, this will consider lighter conductors to try and salvage the 
existing towers. 
 
Alternative 3 - Rebuilding the circuit with wood poles: If the structures are not able to be 
reused and must be replaced, single-circuit wood pole structures will be considered.  
 
Alternative 4 - System reconfiguration: This alternative is not feasible as this 
transmission line is required to connect National Grid, RGE and  NYSEG stations. 
 
Alternative 5 - REV solutions: Cannot be implemented as these assets are still necessary 
to support the transmission system.

Program Name:  
Conductor Clearance 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
The Conductor Clearance program will increase the clearance of certain overhead 
conductors to address locations that may not meet standards prescribed by the National 
Electrical Safety Code (“NESC”) under certain loading conditions. The need for greater 
clearances has been identified as a result of an ongoing Aerial Laser Survey (ALS), also 
known as LiDAR for Light Detection and Ranging, being conducted on the transmission 
system. Clearances are in the process of being measured with aerial surveys providing an 
accuracy which was previously available by ground inspection only.  The program will 
continue beyond FY22 to address conductor clearance issues for 115kV lines.  This 
timeline assumes there will be no further directives from FERC similar to the October 7, 
2010 NERC Alert (Recommendation to Industry: Consideration of Actual Field 
Conditions in Determination of Facility Ratings) that would prescribe a specific 
correction period. 
 
To minimize the need for Part 102 filings, circuits within a common corridor are bundled 
together and undergo desktop reviews of ALS data to identify deficient spans that are 
labeled as a ‘point of interest’ (POI).  POI’s/spans that are confirmed in the field as not 
meeting current code requirements for conductor clearance, and where the line cannot be 
re-rated following analysis by Transmission Planning, will be addressed through a variety 
of construction methods; i.e. re-grading, installation of floating dead-ends, re-framing, 
and as a last resort structure replacement.

          Page 83 of 371

C048678 
Conductor Clearance – NY Program 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Project Justification: 
 
This program assures that transmission lines meet the governing NESC under which they 
were constructed by addressing ground to conductor clearances in substandard spans.  
This follows standard industry practice and a Public Service Commission Order (Case 
04-M-0159, effective January 5, 2005) that the Company shall adhere to the NESC.  The 
NESC sets required conductor clearances of overhead lines from the ground and other 
ground based objects. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
While safety events caused by substandard clearance conductors are rare, their 
consequences can be serious and are difficult to quantify.  Application of the NESC 
criteria provides a reasonable means to manage the issue and mitigate the risk from such 
events. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternatives to correct substandard spans will be handled on a circuit-by-circuit basis.  
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Since this is 
a program, and not a specific project, it was determined that this project will not be 
evaluated for a potential NWA 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Reliability upgrades improve the system's ability to avoid a contingency (hardening, 
flood mitigation), reduce the exposure to contingency (fusing), and/or improve post 
contingency system capacity (MWh violation upgrades). Such benefits create more 
opportunities for renewable energy resources DER (such as PV and ESS) to export 
power, thereby improving the economics of individual projects. Further, improved 
reliability mitigates the need for load customers to operate backup generation, which is 
typically natural gas or petroleum fueled generation.

Description: 
 
The project provides for the installation of a new control building, relays and new cables 
to all of the electrical equipment in the yard. Installing new cables will allow for a quick 
cut over for the new installation and will minimalize outages. The old control building 
will be demolished as part of the Menands project 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Menands is a 115kV, 34.5k, 13.2kV, and 4.16kV transmission substation that ties the 
115kV transmission system to the sub-transmission and distribution systems in the 
Albany area and a key substation for voltage support in the region.  
 
The Menands substation control house and the station relay equipment were identified in 
the approved New York Relay Strategy Paper SG157 as being deteriorated assets and 
obsolete assets with no support from the original equipment manufacturer (OEM).  The 
control house is 80 years old and along with the substation relays are being replaced due 
to asset condition. 
 
The Protection and Telecom Operations personnel have identified several families of 
electromechanical and solid-state relays that are no longer sustainable on the transmission 
system. Further, many of these relays suffer from lack of manufacturer support such that

technical support and spare parts are no longer available. The targeted relays were

The Menands control house was selected for replacement due to inadequate environment 
for microprocessor relays, and because the existing building is not of adequate size to

Customer Benefit: 
 
The planned replacement of the substation assets reduces the likelihood of an in-service 
failure of relay protective systems which are essential to minimize the impact of a fault 
which can lead to long-term interruptions of the transmission system as well as customer 
outages. 
 
Alternatives:

would install new equipment in an existing building that would have a shorter life span 
then the newly installed assets and does not allow for expansion. 
 
Do Nothing: This is not recommended since this would mean leaving the equipment in a 
deteriorated condition and would create additional maintenance issues and allow for the 
possibility of a larger spread resulting from a fault. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative:

history of leaks from the Oil filled equipment, mechanism issues, limited spare parts, 
limited to no Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support, and disconnects 
indicating hot spots.

manufactured by Allis-Chalmers in 1958.

(TB#2) was manufactured by Westinghouse Corporation in 1958, and transformer #3 
(TR#3) was manufactured by Magnetek Electric in 1993.  The TB#2 has only a spare 
phase unit on site and no other available units, no OEM support, and has a history of

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers: C060240, C074000, C074485 and C074489 
 
Description: 
 
The project scope includes the relocation of the Inghams 115/46/13.2kV substation to a 
new greenfield location in close proximity to the existing site, but above the 500-year 
flood zone.  The existing phase angle regulator (PAR), which moderates the power flow 
on the local 115kV lines, will be replaced with a unit offering greater range which is 
planned to be purchased as a spare in advance of this project under a separate project 
(C047864 Inghams Phase Shifting Transformer).  The existing unit will then be made 
available as a spare.   
 
 The project will also extend the 115kV transmission lines approximately one-half mile 
each to the new site, as well as build an approximately one-half mile of 46kV line to 
reconnect to Brookfield to the system. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Ingham’s substation is located at a shared facility with Brookfield Power.  There are 
two locations at this facility that house the relay and protection controls for the National 
Grid owned equipment.  One is the National Grid owned control house which was 
installed to house the equipment that supports and the Phase Angle Regulator (PAR) 
itself, and the other is the Brookfield owned Power House.

The protection relays are obsolete within the Brookfield Powerhouse and have limited/no 
spare parts, limited/no Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support. (manufactured 
in 1952) 
 
There are nine (9) 115kV Oil Circuit Breakers (OCB) that are large OCBs and have had a 
history of leaks, mechanism issues, lack spare parts and have no/limited Original 
Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support.  There are six (6) Westinghouse type GM 
OCBs that have a family issue identified in the NY OCB replacement strategy and were 
manufactured in 1952. There are three (3) Siemens Allis-Chalmers OCBs that were 
manufactured in 1978, to support the installation of the PAR. 
 
The PAR was reviewed from a transmission planning study and a new PAR was 
recommended with a larger range of operations to support system requirements. The 
existing PAR would be kept as a spare at the new land location in-case the new one 
experiences a failure.  The original PAR was manufactured by Westinghouse Electric in 
1978. 
 
The remaining 115kV asset concerns are the nineteen (19) manual gang-operated 
disconnects, and the 90 cap and pin insulators. Which were manufactured in 1952. The 
cap and pin insulators have a history of failures do to the cement core deteriorating over 
time due to the fluctuations in weather. 
 
The substation has 115kV vertical bus as compared to horizontal bus which is a safety 
concern to work on and around since it limits working space per its design, and parallels 
both buses near each other. 
 
In addition, the relocation will provide for the separation of assets between the National 
Grid substation and the interconnected Brookfield hydro facility.  Presently, National 
Grid has shared assets that reside in the Brookfield owned powerhouse at the Inghams 
site 
 
Due to the 2006 flood, it is planned to relocate the substation approximately a quarter 
mile towards the west of the existing site. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The planned replacement of this substation reduces the likelihood of an in-service failure 
of deteriorated equipment which can lead to long-term interruptions of the transmission 
system as well as customer outages. It also serves to separate the assets between National 
Grid and Brookfield.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  C084293 
 
Description: 
 
This project replaces  TB1 & TB3 with one 30/40/50 MVA transformer add 3V0 and a 
bus tie breaker on 115kV bus and  installs  a permanent 115kV 22.5 MVAr, and replaces 
the station fence.  In addition, a 115kV switch is to be installed in Line 116 to function as 
a bypass during circuit breaker maintenance.    
 
Project Justification: 
 
Transformers TB1& TB3 (69-34.5kV) are vintage 1930's and are in deteriorated physical 
condition.. Furthermore, a single contingency (N-1) of 115kV Mortimer-Golah Line 110 
outage will cause TB1 & TB3 to be loaded at 105% of Long Term Emergency rating. In 
addition, a bus outage will interrupt power to approximately 22,000 customers.  Also, 
Line 116 is radial to North Lakeville and it is difficult to remove from service for 115kV 
breaker maintenance. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Addressing TB1 &TB3 asset condition issues and  overloads during contingencies will 
reduce constraints on the Transmission and Sub Transmission systems. The larger size 
transformer allows for expansion of renewable generation in this area. Adding a bus tie 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 98 of 371

Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
breaker and Line 116 bypass switch will allow for operational flexibility and increase 
reliability.  
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Replace TB1 &TB3 in kind, add 3V0, and install a bus tie breaker. 
Replacing the transformers with the same size puts TB1 and TB3 at risk of overload and 
would risk unplanned outages and delays. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Due to the 
timing of the need, it was determined that this project will not be evaluated for a potential 
NWA.    
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Load relief upgrades directly increase the maximum hosting capacity of the local EPS 
(electric power system) by two mechanisms. Increased asset capacity allows for a higher 
reverse power flow. Additionally, it allows more load to interconnect, which generally 
increases the threshold for certain higher cost interconnection upgrades (such as 3V0). 
This will enable PV and ESS to interconnect at higher volumes with a lower marginal 
interconnection cost. VVO directly contributes to system efficiency, contributing to EE 
targets, as well as reducing energy required from carbon heavy generation (by reducing 
the total energy procured from NYISO). Increasing efficiency also reduces peak loading, 
which may decrease the need for fossil fuel peaking plants. Transmission upgrades will 
eliminate congestions and allow for a more lower cost clean energy to reach load centers.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  C082919 
 
Description: 
 
This project provides for the replacement of the 115kV and 34.5kV deteriorated assets 
which includes two (2) transformer banks TB1 and TB2 and their associated protection 
and control devices.  Also included is the replacement of six (6) 34.5kV vacuum circuit 
breakers (VCB) and their associated protection and control devices.  The replacement of 
18 surge arrestors, 24 bus supports, and one (1) station service transformer will also be 
replaced, a new control house will be installed with IEC-61850 communications 
protocol.   
 
Project Justification: 
 
The existing station transformers are being replaced due to their asset condition.  An asset 
condition report in January 2014 noted that they are showing signs of deterioration 
through various in service and diagnostic data.  These transformers are also on the asset 
replacement list.  The transformers supply power to the 34.5kV switchyard across Albany 
Street via wood pole and crossarm structures which appear to be very old.  The asset 
condition report and site visit cataloged several other conditions within the substation 
which should be remediated.  Obsolete transformer protection, insulators, bus arrestors, 
work lighting, lightning protection, collapsed control cable conduits from the control 
house to the 115kV yard, and electrical distribution deficiencies will also be addressed.  
Station service is currently supplied via two transformer banks, 3 and 6.  They are in poor

will be replaced with a simpler design, allowing for the retirement of the 2.4kV bus and 
structures.  In addition, this scope includes station work prescribed by the strategy 
documents for replacement of the 34.5kV Butyl Rubber PT’s and the obsolete relaying on 
the #35 line.   
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The project will replace an assets in poor condition that will maintain the reliability of the 
system. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Replacement of 115kV and 34.5kV assets with an underground option instead of 
overhead option to connect the low-side of the power transformers to the 34.5kV bus 
across the street. This option was not chosen due to the existing overhead conductor still 
being in good condition. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
As the project is driven by asset condition, it does not meet the NWA suitability criteria 
thresholds.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  C081115 
 
Description: 
 
This project replaces the 115kV, 34.5kV, and 13.2kV degraded  assets , which include 
the two (2) power transformers, two (2) 115kV disconnect switches, thirty-three (33) cap 
and pin insulators, four (4) Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs), and protection relays.  This also 
includes a new control house utilizing IEC-61850.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Hoosick substation assets listed below  are in  deteriorated condition, lack of spare 
parts and Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support, and prone to mechanism 
failures.   
 
The 115kV assets with condition concerns   include; approximately six (6) cap and pin 
insulators, and two (2) disconnect switches.  The 34.5kV assets with condition concerns 
include; approximately fifteen (15) of cap and pin insulators, six (6) disconnect switches, 
and two (2) Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs).  The 13.2kV with condition concerns include 
approximately twelve (12) cap and pin insulators, and two (2) OCBs.   
 
The 115kV – 34.5kV transformer and the 115kV – 13.2V transformer have indications of 
deterioration; gassing and high levels of acetylene.

Program Name:

Description: 
 
This project includes the replacement of the 34.5kV and 115kV assets including 
transformers  TB#1, TB#2, seven (7) 34.5kV Oil Circuit Breakers(OCB), four (4) 115kV 
OCBs, twenty-four (24) disconnect switches, and seventy-two (72) cap and pin insulators 
The new protection and control scheme will utilize IEC-61850. The station yard will be 
expanded to  accommodate a new control house.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
Most of the 115kV and 34.5kV equipment at Mohican Station is in poor condition with 
limited spare parts, limited Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support, and have 
reoccurring performance issues. There are three (3) 115kV oil circuit breakers (OCBs) 
and seven (7) 34.5kV OCBs still in service and targeted to be replaced as part of New 
York Transmission Oil Circuit Breaker Replacement Strategy. Also there is one (1) gas 
circuit breaker (GCB) that has a history of leaking and operating problems.  The existing 
transformer banks TB#1 and TB#2 are 115-34.5 kV , both of which are degrading and 
have a history of oil leaks and gassing.  
 
The Distribution Planning and Asset Management (DPAM) department has also 
conducted the Moreau Area Study, finding the best option to add one (1) 115kV –

Customer Benefit: 
 
The planned replacement of these substation assets reduces the likelihood of an in-service 
failure of deteriorated assets which can lead to long-term interruptions of the transmission 
system as well as customer outages.  
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - The replacement of the 34.5kV and 115kV assets (TB#1, TB#2, seven (7) 
34.5kV OCBs, four (4) 115kV OCBs, twenty-four (24) disconnect switches, and seventy-
two (72) cap and pin insulators) utilizing current methods for protection and control. The 
asset replacement is necessary due degrading equipment, lack of spare parts and lack of 
OEM support. The expansion of the station yard will accommodate a new control house.

Description: 
 
The scope of this project is to rebuild the Lockport-Mortimer #111/#113 taps to 
Brockport Station (3.53 mi/3.5 mi, respectively).  
 
The Brockport taps are constructed with wood (a combination of H-Frames and double 
circuits on single-wood poles). The conductor is 4/0 ACSR and there is no shield wire 
present. 
 
As part of the project, the entire 111/113 Brockport Taps will be evaluated in an aerial 
comprehensive inspection, wire samples will be harvested to be destructively tested for 
strength and corrosion, and the wire will be non-destructively tested using the Kinectrics 
LineVue. 
 
Upon evaluation of the components, the line will be rebuilt using direct embedded steel 
H-Frame structures and 795 ACSR 26/7 “Drake” or equivalent hybrid conductor. OPGW 
(Optical Ground Wire) will be installed in a shield wire position.

C055531 
Brockport Tap ACR 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Approximately 6 years ago, the Lockport-Mortimer #111 mainline was rebuilt, along 
with a partial rebuild of the #113 & #114 mainline. The insulators and shield wire were 
replaced at the time; however, the taps received no attention.  
 
The Lockport-Mortimer #111/113/114 are collectively poor performing circuits. Since 
2013, the Lockport-Mortimer #111 has experienced 24 disturbances, and the #113 has 
experienced 19 disturbances. There are a large number of customers that are supplied by 
these circuits; the #111 has 22,961 customers at risk and the #113 has 21,588 customers 
at risk. Of the total customer count on each circuit, the Brockport taps supply 16,996 of 
the customers. 
 
The wood poles on the Brockport tap between Brockport Station and West Hamlin 
station (Double Circuits on Single-Wood Poles) were evaluated by Osmose in 2018 
following a pole fire. Several poles with woodpecker damage were found during this 
inspection, needing replacement. The similar vintage and construction wood poles on the 
Brockport taps will be evaluated to confirm condition. 
 
After the recent rebuild of the Alabama-Telegraph #115 tap in early 2019, the conductor 
on the adjacent Lockport-Mortimer #114 Telegraph Road Tap was harvested for 
destructive testing (Similar vintage, conductor type, and construction). A total of 5 
samples of the 4/0 Penguin 6/1 ACSR were harvested and sent to the National Grid 
Worchester Lab for testing. In reviewing the tensile strength test results, the steel core 
tested well while (6) aluminum strands contributed to the failing results. The corrosion 
analysis evaluated the minimum thickness of zinc. Of the 5 samples evaluated, one 
sample marginally passed by 0.00001-inches. Further conductor testing on the Brockport 
taps will confirm the condition of the conductor. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to provide reliable service to customers served by 
National Grid.  This overhead line refurbishment program promotes safety and reliability 
by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the 
governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by 
replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC.

Alternatives:

• Conductor deemed insufficient for capacity would be replaced. Conductor

shield wire will also be replaced with OPGW  
 
 
Alternative 3 - Total Rebuild (Hybrid Conductor) (Preferred Option)  
 
Same as Alternative 2 above with the exception of a new hybrid ACSS or ACCC 
conductor. The hybrid conductor has the potential to decrease the total number of 
structures per mile as compared to ACSR; thus, decreasing the corresponding cost per 
mile for the ACR

Description: 
 
This project addresses the 115kV SE Batavia – Golah #119 transmission line segment 
(27.8miles).   Subsequent condition projects being considered within the same area are 
the 115kV Mortimer-Golah #110 (9.58 miles), to the east, and the 115kV Batavia-SE

PowerPlant under the Major Location of Batavia-SE Batavia 117 & 119 dated back to

be non-destructively tested using the HydroQuebec LineCore.  If the conductor tests are

Project Justification: 
 
The #119 line has had eight (8) momentary outages since 4/10/2013.  
 
The #119 line has had a history of failed wood poles. During a late winter wind storm on 
March 8, 2017 (11) round wood poles on the 1.53 mile Lapp Substation loop-in/loop-out 
tap failed as a result of an 81 mph wind gust (measured at the Rochester Airport). The 
poles on this tap are single wood poles supporting a single circuit on horizontal line posts. 
 
There is also approximately 15.31 miles of 397.5 kcmil Aluminum Conductor Steel 
Reinforced (ASCR) (18/1 “Chickadee” or 26/7 “Ibis”) conductor on the mainline.  This 
conductor is considered some of the oldest ACSR that NMPC owns, and appears to have 
been installed in the 1920’s.  
 
As part of the Needs Case to determine if there was a need for a capital project, the entire 
SE Batavia-Golah #119 was aerially inspected and Osmose performed a ground-based 
pole inspection and treatment program.  The aerial inspection resulted in a need for a 
capital project.  Decayed wooden crossarms, flashed insulators, less than standard 
number of insulators, Lapp polymer insulators, and wood poles with woodpecker damage 
were all encountered.   
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
There are a total of 38,675 customers supported from the #119 line and the 115kV 
Mortimer-Golah #110 including the 115kv Golah-North Lakeville #116 which is radially 
supplied from the Golah substation.  
 
Reducing the number of momentary outages on the line could maintain or improve 
reliability for customers. 
 
A refurbishment of this line could also improve safety for the public. Failure of wood 
poles (as seen in 2017) could be avoided with the proposed replacement. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Wood Pole Replacement – Conductor Tests fine:  
 
• As part of Options Selection the conductor will be non-destructively tested using 
the Kinectrics LineVue.  If the conductor tests are acceptable; the conductor can 
remain inservice.

Description: 
 
This project addresses the 115kV Mortimer – Golah #110 transmission line segment

Project Justification: 
 
The mainline contains approximately 5.53 miles of 397.5 kcmil Aluminum Conductor 
Steel Reinforced (ASCR) 18/1 “Chickadee” conductor. This conductor is considered 
some of the oldest ACSR in the NMPC system, appearing to have been installed in the 
1920’s.  
 
As part of the Need Case, the entire SE Batavia-Golah #119 (same vintage/construction) 
was both aerially inspected and received a ground-based pole inspection/treatment 
program by Osmose. The aerial inspection revealed decayed wooden crossarms, flashed 
insulators, Lapp polymer insulators, and wood poles with woodpecker damage. The 
findings of this aerial inspection indicated that a Capital Project should be initiated. 
 
In the spring of 2019, Transmission Asset Management implemented a partial aerial 
comprehensive inspection of the #119 circuit to evaluate the magnitude of wood pecker 
damage identified by I&M. The results showed severe woodpecker damage to the wood 
poles. It is suspected that the same conditions are present on the #110 line due to similar 
location and construction/vintage. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The #110 circuit is part of a redundant feed to supply Golah Station (115kV:34.5kV) 
substation), supporting the supply of 38,675 customers. The 115kV Golah-North 
Lakeville #116 extends radially  from the Golah Station. The #110 is critical to ensure 
that customers supplied from Golah Station are supplied in the event that the #119 line is 
out-of-service.  
 
A refurbishment of this line could also improve safety for the public. Failure of wood 
poles (as seen in 2017 on the #119 line) could be avoided with the proposed replacement. 
 
Alternatives:

The scope of this option is to address wood poles and/or structures identified by aerial 
inspection as requiring replacement.  The replacements will be direct-embedded steel 
poles with steel cross arms and toughened glass insulators 
 
• Polymer insulators would also be replaced with the standard toughened glass 
insulators

Program Name: 
345kV Laminated Cross-Arms 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
The D-1501-type 345kV structures built prior to 1975 will be aerially inspected to 
identify delaminating cross-arms and overstressed vee braces.  The aerial inspection will 
be scheduled over a number of years with road crossing inspected initially followed by 
the remaining off-road structures.  Those circuits with a history of delaminated cross-
arms have been previously addressed. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The New Scotland – Alps #2 T5450 345kV line has experienced two cross arm failures, 
one in 2012 and a second in 2014. Both were on tangent (NMPC Overhead Electric 
Transmission Standards D-1501-type) structures - a two-pole wood H-frame with two 
laminated wood cross-arms and wood vee braces.  The root cause has been identified as 
delamination of the wood layers that make up the laminated cross arms used to support 
the suspension insulators.  These specific laminated cross arms manufactured by Joslyn 
were used by Niagara Mohawk on all 345kV circuits prior to approximately 1975. 
 
Several D1501 cross arm samples were obtained from structures that were being 
replaced on the T5450 New Scotland-Alps #2 line due to normal maintenance. These 
cross arms were destructively examined in the field by forcing a shear failure parallel to 
their laminations.  Once split, the lamination was examined for glue adhesion quality.  
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 128 of 371


--- Page 279 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 129 of 371 
C060365 
345kV Laminated Cross Arm 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Concurrently, full sized cross arm samples were sent to the State University of New York 
College of Environmental Science and Forestry (SUNY-ESF) for laboratory analysis to 
measure their bending strength and compare them to their original design specifications.  
The results found the in-service cross arms were weaker than specifications. 
 
Follow-up to the SUNY-ESF testing consisted of an aerial inspection program to identify 
deteriorated cross arms and overstressed vee braces in the field for D-1501 structures 
constructed prior to 1975. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
This program enhances public safety by replacing damaged or failed transmission 
overhead line components prior to failure.  Replacing damaged or failed components on 
345kV also enhance system reliability as these circuits are heavily loaded and when de-
energized for maintenance, typically results in congestion costs and additional loading on 
other 345kV circuits.  
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1- Replace the laminated cross arms as damage/failure work: This action is 
not recommended on the 345kV system because it potentially places the public at risk.  In 
addition, a fault on the 345kV places stress on the other 345kV lines in the region and 
may cause de-rating of other 345kV lines when they are most needed. 
 
Alternative 2 - Rely on the visual I&M Program to detect delaminated cross arms: This 
action is not recommended as the delaminated cross arms are not easily detected from the 
ground. 
 
Alternative 3 - REV solutions: Cannot be implemented as these assets are still necessary 
to support the transmission system. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative:   
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Since this is 
a program, and not a specific project, it was determined that this project will not be 
evaluated for a potential NWA 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA): N/A

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers: C082332, C082668, C046418 
 
Description: 
 
The Malone Area Study looked at solving Asset Condition issues and all MWhr 
violations at Malone Substation and the surrounding stations.  To eliminate the MWhr 
violations and all asset condition issues it is necessary to retire Elm Street and North 
Bangor substations, install a second bank at Malone substation and transfer the load from 
Elm St. and N. Bangor onto the second bank.   
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Malone Area Study looked at solving Asset Condition issues and all MWhr 
violations at Malone Substation and the surrounding stations.  Currently upon loss of the 
bank at Malone there would be approximately 400 MWhrs at risk, violating the 240 
MWhr criteria.  Malone is a 13.2kV island with no adequate neighboring feeder ties. The 
Malone station feeds 3,791 customers. In 2018, an Inspection report that was completed 
on Elm St., North Bangor, and Malone Stations.  This inspection report identified the 3- 
phase regulator at Elm Street, the Metal Clad at Malone, and the North Bangor TB1 and 
breakers needing replacement.

Page 133 of 371 
C069306 
Malone Substation Rebuild_T_Sub 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
This will eliminate all MWHr violations at Malone Substation, all asset condition issues 
at Malone, Elm St., and N. Bangor substations, eliminate the maintenance costs from Elm 
St and N Bangor substations, and adds distributed generation hosting capacity to the 
Malone area. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
The second alternative is to fix the asset condition issues at Elm St. substation, Convert 
N. Bangor substation to 13.2kV, and replace the Metalclad at Malone.  This option 
eliminates all the asset condition issues but leaves 192MWhr's at risk which is 
approximately 3,500 customers out of power upon loss the Malone substation. The third 
option is to convert Elm St. substation to 13.2kV, convert N. Bangor substation to 
13.2kV and replace the Metalclad at Malone substation.  This option eliminates all asset 
condition issues but leaves 120MWhr's at risk which is approximately 2,200 customers 
out of power upon loss of Malone substation. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
No DER/NWA alternative solutions may be utilized for this project since the substation 
asset is still needed as part of the system and NWA solutions do not address the asset 
condition issues. 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Load relief upgrades directly increase the maximum hosting capacity of the local EPS 
(electric power system) by two mechanisms. Increased asset capacity allows for a higher 
reverse power flow. Additionally, it allows more load to interconnect, which generally 
increases the threshold for certain higher cost interconnection upgrades (such as 3V0). 
This will enable PV and ESS to interconnect at higher volumes with a lower marginal 
interconnection cost. VVO directly contributes to system efficiency, contributing to EE 
targets, as well as reducing energy required from carbon heavy generation (by reducing 
the total energy procured from NYISO). Increasing efficiency also reduces peak loading, 
which may decrease the need for fossil fuel peaking plants. Transmission upgrades will 
eliminate congestions and allow for a more lower cost clean energy to reach load centers.

Project Justification:

centers and the substations. The existing protocol for some RTUs does not match the 
control center protocol and can lead to a loss of communications. This would affect the 
remote operability of the equipment and require personnel to be dispatched to the 
substation to operate the equipment.

Program Name:  
None 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  C078287 and C079071 
 
Description: 
 
 This project is to reconductor 3.0 miles of double circuit 336.4 kcmil ACSR in the 
115kV Maplewood-Menands #19  and 115kV Maplewood-Reynolds #31 lines.  The 
associated projects replace equipment at the substations that would otherwise limit the 
circuits. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The #19 and #31 circuits are exposed to post-contingency overloading during summer 
peak conditions. The proposed reconductoring will relieve these circuits from exposure to 
the most limiting N-1-1 scenarios. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Relieving the #19 line for the worst-case N-1-1 contingency would require approximately 
95MW of load to be shed. Relieving the #31 line for the worst-case N-1-1 contingency 
would require approximately 89MW of load to be shed from the same part of the 
transmission system. The total load shed required represents approximately 56,000 
residential customers which the proposed project would benefit directly.

Alternatives: 
 
Extending a new circuit from a station which is not already fed by the loops which the 
#19 and #31 are part of (Menands, or North Troy; for instance): This would be more 
expensive and time-consuming compared with the recommended reinforcement. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Based on the 
Company’s evaluation, the need addressed by this project does not satisfy one or more 
element of the Suitability Criteria and will not be evaluated for a potential NWA. 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Load relief upgrades directly increase the maximum hosting capacity of the local EPS 
(electric power system) by two mechanisms. Increased asset capacity allows for a higher 
reverse power flow. Additionally, it allows more load to interconnect, which generally 
increases the threshold for certain higher cost interconnection upgrades (such as 3V0). 
This will enable PV and ESS to interconnect at higher volumes with a lower marginal 
interconnection cost. VVO directly contributes to system efficiency, contributing to EE 
targets, as well as reducing energy required from carbon heavy generation (by reducing 
the total energy procured from NYISO). Increasing efficiency also reduces peak loading, 
which may decrease the need for 'dirty' peaker plants. Transmission upgrades will 
eliminate congestions and allow for a more lower cost clean energy to reach load centers.

Description:

western side of the existing Clay 115kV yard. A new 115kV breaker will be

Project Justification: 
 
The LHH-Clay #7 is presently a 26.53-mile bussed 115kV circuit.  The Lighthouse Hill-
Clay #7 is one of the Worst Performing NY circuits.  In response to the number of 
momentary outages on the 7-circuit, an aerial comprehensive inspection was 
commissioned to documents defects.   Defects found were generally: 
 
• Several flashed insulators 
• Several broken insulators 
• Elongated vangs 
• Corroded shield wire.  Note the 7 line has two shield wires 
• Corroded steel structures 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
This project is aimed to improve reliability and decrease the number and duration of 
interruptions to customers. Additional benefits of this project will be replacement of 
assets that have failed.  The conductor clearance portion will improve safety by 
correcting deficiently sagged spans. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Life Extension/Refurbishment 
Based on the recent aerial comprehensive inspection this targeted life extension 
refurbishment project would include the following at a minimum: 
 
Replace both overhead shield wires  
Replace the flashed insulators.  If replacing only one string, all strings get replaced 
together with the vangs 
Perform a conductor clearance evaluation on the circuit 
Evaluate if painting will extend the life of the structures as well 
 
The intent of this option is to provide a minimum of 20 additional years to the asset life 
in-order for other Planning and Capacity projects to be advanced.   
 
Alternative 2 - Asset Condition Refurbishment 
 
This option is the classic refurbishment.  Replace the existing structures with direct-
embedded steel for tangents and steel poles on concrete foundations for dead ends.  New 
structures to receive new insulators, and new shield wire; either one or two.  The shield 
wire would be Optical Ground Wire (OPGW).  The new LHH-Clay #7 would not be a

Alternative 3 - System Reconfiguration 1 
 
In this option the mainline between LHH and the Clay substation will be reconfigured to 
supply  the two National Grid substations another way.  Mallory Substation is presently 
1.68-miles north of the intersection of the South Oswego-Clay #4. The S. Oswego-Clay 
#4 is also being proposed for refurbishment, but at a later date.  This option is to supply 
the Mallory substation from the S. Oswego-Clay #4 with a single circuit direct embedded 
steel pole line and at the tap point a three-ring breaker substation will be installed to 
improve the  reliability of the substation. 
 
Wetzel Rd Substation is presently supplied from the LHH-Clay #7 Wetzel Rd Tap.  The 
Wetzel Rd Tap extends from the Clay substation 3.57 miles south.  The LHH-Clay #7 
Wetzel Rd Tap is double circuited with the Clay-General Electric #14.  At a point due 
south of the Clay substation (approximately 2,000-ft), a new 115kV circuit will tie the 
Clay substation to the double circuit supplying Wetzel Rd substation.  At Clay substation 
there is a spare bay that would need to be developed in order for the new Wetzel Rd 
supply line to be connected. 
 
The system reconfiguration will take several years to implement.  Immediate condition-
based issues will be addressed and prioritized to maintain or even enhance customers 
reliability on the 7 line prior to the system reconfiguration 
 
DER/NWA Alternative:   
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Since the 
justification for this project is Asset Condition in nature, it was determined that this 
project will not be evaluated for a potential NWA.

Project Justification: 
 
This 23.4 mile line is of 1900s vintage and is in need of refurbishment. The steel lattice 
towers are in need of inspection and paint to extend its useful life. The circuit is still 
using deteriorating brown porcelain insulators which need to be replaced. The steel shield 
wire needs to be harvested and tested for rated breaking strength, possibly requiring 
replacement. Towers and poles will be inspected and replaced as needed. 
 
The 38/39 circuits both have 23,330 customers at risk. Since 2012, the 38 line has 
experienced (6) outages and the 39 line has (10) experienced outages. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to provide reliable service to customers served by 
National Grid.  This overhead line refurbishment program promotes safety and reliability 
by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the 
governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by 
replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Refurbishment  (Wire Tests Good) 
 
In this Alternative:  
 
• Structures deemed Reject would be replaced  
• All insulators and hardware would be replaced with toughened glass  
• Conductor will be evaluated and remain in service if passed 
• Shield wire would be evaluated and remain in service if passed 
Alternative 2 - Targeted Refurbishment  (Wire Tests Bad) (Preferred Alternative) 
 
In this Alternative:  
 
• Structures deemed Reject would be replaced  
• All insulators and hardware would be replaced with toughened glass  
• Conductor will be evaluated and replaced if bad 
• Shield wire would be evaluated and replaced if bad

electrically conform to the NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Refurbishment: This alternative replaces deteriorated structures, 
insulators and hardware, adds improved grounding, and targeted replacement of 
conductor and shield wire on the mainline and taps. 
 
Alterative 2 - Line Rebuild: If the conductor fails testing and it is deemed the steel 
structures are too deteriorated to remain in service, the circuit will need to be rebuilt. 
 
Alternative 3 - Substation reconfiguration: At the two customer substations, Whitaker and 
Gilbert Mills, breakers could be installed at the substations to create a ring bus.

DER/NWA Alternative:

determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Since the 
justification for this project is Asset Condition in nature, it was determined that this 
project will not be evaluated for a potential NWA.

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program - Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers: N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This asset condition project will address asset condition issues on the Border City-
Elbridge #10 115kV line, and the Auburn-Elbridge #5 115kV line. 
 
Specifically, the #10 line will receive attention on the National Grid owned section from 
the NYSEG Border City Tap to the NYSEG Auburn/State St Tap. The #10 line runs on 
double circuit towers with the retired “Mortimer-Solvay” circuit. Both circuits (#10 and 
the retired line) will receive attention to ensure safety. 
 
The #5 line will receive attention on the National Grid owned section from the NYSEG 
Auburn/State St Tap to the Elbridge Station. The section of line is “bussed” and runs on 
double circuit steel towers. Both sides of the towers (Both lines of the bussed circuit) will 
receive attention. 
 
The following are details regarding the circuit: 
 
Total length: Border City-Elbridge #10: 25 miles 
Auburn-Elbridge #5: 14.25 miles  
Conductor Types: 336.4 kcm ACSR 30/7 “Oriole”  
Types of structures: Double circuit steel flex towers for tangents and double circuit steel 
square base towers for dead-ends 
Installation Date: 1907 (earliest date in PowerPlant) 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 164 of 371


--- Page 315 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment

C075723 
Border City – Elbridge #10/#5 ACR 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
 
The #10 and #5 lines will undergo a critical crossing reinforcement project. 
Significant/critical crossings will be reconductored (in kind) with new conductor. 
Insulators and hardware will be changed. Structures that are not fit to be re-used will be 
replaced at either side of the crossing. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
There  have been some conductor failures as a result of deteriorated steel core stands in 
recent years. The conductor is over 100 years old, and wire testing has shown signs of 
strength loss over the years of operation. The similar vintage and conductor #4/4A line 
has experienced conductor failure as recent as January 2020. 
 
To mitigate risk of a significant wire failure in the future, alternatives have been 
evaluated. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The #10 circuit serves National Grid’s Elbridge station which ties with the Pannell-
Geneva #4/#4A to transmit power cross-state.  The #10 line serves two NYSEG stations - 
Border City and Hyatt Rd. 
 
The #10 circuit is a key element in the west-east power flow of the 115kV transmission 
network. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Critical Road Crossings Replacement (Preferred): The scope of this option 
is to replace conductor, suspension structures, and insulators/hardware at critical road 
crossings (County Road and above). This alternative will provide confidence that a 
conductor failure will not cause a safety concern for the public. 
 
Alternative 2 - Complete Rebuild of the circuit with 795 ACSR on Direct Embedded 
Steel Poles for tangents, and Steel monopole son foundations for dead ends. 
 
Alternative 3 - System reconfiguration: This alternative is not feasible for an asset 
condition type project.  However, if NYSEG and/or RGE were to construct their own 
cross-state lines the scope of this project could be reevaluated.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
The replacement of the five (5) 115kV Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs) at Batavia Substation 
designated R35, R40, R64, R80 and R90. This work will include the disconnects 
associated with the OCBs and foundation work. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The replacement of problematic, poor condition, large oil volume circuit breakers with 
modern SF6 circuit breakers will improve reliability. The OCBs designated R80 and R64 
are manufactured by General Electric and are FK Types.  The OCBs designated R90, R35 
and R40 are manufactured by Westinghouse and are BZO types. The circuit breakers 
addressed in this Capital Investment Plan (“Plan”) are obsolete, in a state requiring 
replacement, and have limited spare parts or manufacturer support. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
This project will replace assets that are in poor condition. The proactive replacement of 
these assets will limit the likelihood of an in-service failure, which would result in a long-
term outage for many customers.

Description: 
 
This project replaces two (2) 115-34.5kV transformers, four (4) 115kV circuit breakers, 
two (2) 115kV circuit switchers, six (6) 34.5kV circuit breakers, the 34.5kV capacitor 
bank and capacitor switcher as well as lightning arrestors, protection and control 
packages for the 115kV and 34.5kV.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Homer Hill substation is a 115kV – 34.5kV switching yard that has eight (8) 115kV 
transmission lines and three (3) 34.5kV distribution lines. It is designed as an open-air 
straight bus design for both the 115kV and 34.5kV yards.  The two (2) transformers are 
tied on either side of the 115kV and 34.5kV tie bus circuit breakers. 
 
This substation is in the Southwestern region of the New York Service territory. The 
substation was originally constructed in 1950. The substation is part of the 115kV loop 
for the NY southwestern service territory and serves as a connection point between local 
generation and to serve local substations.   
 
There are four (4) 115kV Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs) that have limited/no spare parts, 
no Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support, and problematic mechanisms.
