Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
The Transmission Control Center (TCC) has advised of the operational importance of 
maintaining full load break capabilities with key switches. This program will address the 
replacement of switches that no longer operate as designed and are considered to be a 
priority by the TCC.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Transmission Control Center has notified Asset Management of a number of 
overhead line switches which are operationally important for reliability that have been 
yellow-tagged as being inoperable or difficult to operate. Leaving tagged switches 
inoperable for long periods of time, or removing them, leaves the transmission system 
operationally less flexible. In some cases, this is not acceptable for emergency system 
operations.  
 
The Company has formed a NY Transmission Line Priority Switch Replacement team 
which meets monthly to discuss line switches on the system that have been experiencing 
operational issues and are a priority to the TCC. This switch replacement program is 
targeted for the replacement of three switches per year as required.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
To lessen continued line interruptions on the Company’s transmission network due to the 
growing population of Ospreys between the months of April – September, when they are 
active in New York State,  the Osprey Mitigation/Avian Protection Program  adds nesting 
platforms either to existing structures or adjacent wood poles and transfers nests to those 
platforms.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
Ospreys are birds of prey that build large nests of sticks atop transmission structures 
which can reach 4 – 7 feet in diameter and similar height. The nests typically weigh four 
hundred pounds, although larger ones have been reported at up to seven hundred pounds. 
Interruptions can occur when the nests come into contact with energized conductor or the 
bird droppings cause an arc between phase conductors.  
 
There are growing populations of Ospreys in  New York. The Company has addressed 
line outages caused by Ospreys  by adding  platforms atop transmission  structures which  
has become a proven alternative for the Ospreys to nest. Without further monitoring and 
mitigation efforts, interruptions caused by Osprey nests will continue to increase in 
frequency. 
 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 192 of 371


--- Page 343 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 193 of 371 
C076662 
Osprey Mitigation/Avian Protection 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
With  populations increasing in New York,  Ospreys are no longer classified as 
‘endangered’, but they are still considered ‘of special concern’ by the Department of 
Environmental Conservation (“DEC”) and should be protected. An Osprey Mitigation 
Program will reduce the risk of avian related interruptions and improve system reliability. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Targeted nest removal: When a nest reaches a ‘danger’ level it is immediately removed 
by the Company’s Transmission Line Services personnel with permission from the DEC. 
However, there are DEC restrictions as to when Osprey nests can be moved/removed so a 
nest may be growing to becoming a ‘danger’ nest, but not be able to be addressed in time 
before an interruption occurs. Without a mitigation program proactively installing nesting 
platforms or deterrents, it will be difficult to stay ahead of the growing number of danger 
nests. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Based on the 
Company’s evaluation, the need addressed by this project does not satisfy one or more 
element of the Suitability Criteria and will not be evaluated for a potential NWA. 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Reliability upgrades improve the system's ability to avoid a contingency (hardening, 
flood mitigation), reduce the exposure to contingency (fusing), and/or improve post 
contingency system capacity (MWh violation upgrades). Such benefits create more 
opportunities for renewable energy resources DER (such as PV and ESS) to export 
power, thereby improving the economics of individual projects. Further, improved 
reliability mitigates the need for load customers to operate backup generation, which is 
typically natural gas or petroleum fueled generation.

Program Name: 
Public Requirements (additional need) 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project consists of a 1.25-mile customer requested relocation of the 115kV Lafarge-
Pleasant Valley #8 / 115kV Feura Bush-North Catskill #2 between T#52 and T#63 (T#53 
through T#62 to be removed). The relocation includes the addition of (14) structures 
which include (8) tangent and light angle structures and (6) dead-end type structures.  It 
also includes the removal of (10) existing lattice structures.  The new alignment is 
approximately 1.40-miles in length. 
 
The tangent and light angle structures will be direct-embedded engineered steel poles 
supporting the double circuit 115kV lines.  The dead-end structures will be steel poles 
supported on concrete drilled shaft piers.  Dead-end structures will be used at the two 
transition locations between the new circuit and the old circuit and at higher line angle 
locations.  Conductor will be 795 26/7 ACSR “Drake” with steel shield wire. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
NMPC executed a relocation agreement with Atlantic Cement, the predecessor to 
LaFarge-Holcim US LTD, in 1962. This agreement stipulated that Atlantic Cement 
would provide NMPC with “a new right of way in fee of the same width and 
approximately the same length as its existing right of way and suitable for right of way 
purposes and at no cost to Niagara and Niagara agrees within twelve months thereafter to 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 199 of 371


--- Page 350 ---

Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 200 of 371 
C079454 
Lafarge Relocation 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
relocate the tower line on the new right of way and to convey to Atlantic its present right 
of way in fee.”  
 
The agreement stipulates that the cost of relocating the tower line (other than the cost of 
the new right of way) will be as follows:  
 
• For the initial fifteen years, between July 1, 1962 and 6/30/1977, Atlantic would 
pay 100% of the relocation costs  
 
• Between 15 (7/1/1977) years and 50 years (6/30/2012), Atlantic would pay 50% 
of the relocation costs  
 
• After 50 year (7/1/2012), the entire cost of relocation is born by NMPC  
The tower line being referred to is the 115kV Feura Bush-North Catskill #2 /115kV 
LaFarge-Pleasant Valley #8.  
 
In late 2017, LaFarge notified NMPC that they were exercising their rights in the 1962 
agreement and requested the tower line to be relocated. In the fall of 2017, NMPC met 
on-site with LaFarge’s Plant Manager and their consultant to outline what was required. 
According to the agreement, the portion of the transmission line covered by this 
agreement is 1.93 miles. The new alignment proposed by LaFarge is 7,179-ft. (1.36 
miles), replacing the mainline segment from approximately Str. 53 to Str. 62 (1.19 miles).  
 
Under the NMPC-Atlantic Cement agreement, the proposed tower line relocation is at 
National Grid’s expense. However, the agreement stipulates that LaFarge is to provide 
NMPC with a suitable new right of way. The project team has provided LaFarge with 
standard requirements for a suitable right of way. As of November 2018 Lafarge, agreed 
to work on the suitable right of way if National Grid agreed to work concurrently on the 
line relocation.  
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The benefit to the customer is the access to additional mining land that the 115kV lines 
currently reside on within their property. The mining operations are moving closer to the 
area where the lines are located, and Lafarge has notified National Grid that their 
production will be adversely affected without these lines relocated. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
NMPC has no other option besides relocation. However, we have several Alternatives

Description: 
 
The replacement of ten (10) OCBs, three (3) CVTs (Capacitive Voltage Transformers), 
five (5) disconnect switches, and twelve (12) Surge Arresters utilizing the current 
protection equipment 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Albany Steam substation has ten (10) 115kV OCBs (Oil filled Circuit Breakers) still 
in service that are in poor condition, lack OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) 
support, have mechanism issues, and are part of the New York Transmission Oil Circuit 
Breaker Replacement Strategy. Five (5) 115 kV disconnect switches with problematic 
cap and pin insulators,  three (3) CVTs (Capacitive Voltage Transformers) and twelve 
(12) surge arresters are to be replaced due to poor condition and reliability concerns.   
The remaining assets at the substation are presently in good condition and are not planned 
for replacement.  The Albany Steam facility is a shared facility with PSE&G.  The 
National Grid owned protection and control assets are located within its own building 
next to the substation yard.

Program Name:

Description: 
 
This project replaces approximately of 3.4 miles of conductor with 2156 kcmil 84/19 
ACSS “Bluebird” conductor, replacement of one 2000/1200-5A Bushing CT and one 
2000/1000-5A Bushing CT to bring Packard thermal ratings to a 3000 Amp Short Term 
Emergency (STE) rating.  No structures on the 3.4 mile stretch are expected to be 
replaced as they were previously replaced or reinforced when the other half of this double 
circuit (Niagara-Packard 195) was reconductored.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
The 115kV Niagara – Packard 192 line is overloaded under certain system conditions and 
is a limiting factor for the amount of power imported from Ontario and generated within 
NY at the Niagara/Lewiston facility.  The overloads occur for N-1 and N-1-1 outages of 
parallel facilities that provide generation exits from Niagara.  The maximum N-1 loading 
was 352MVA (99% of conductor (STE), (STE allowed per New York State Reliability 
Council Exception 13) and the maximum N-1-1 loading was 383MVA (108% of STE).  
All conductor between Niagara and Packard was found to be overloaded. The N-1 
loading on this facility for design contingencies surpasses the STE rating of the 
conductor.  Operating the lines within their rating would require reductions at the 
Niagara/Lewiston facility and reductions to the Ontario imports.  The limitations set by 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6)

Niagara-Packard 192 Reconductor

thermal ratings on these lines, constrain the initiative for increased clean energy in New 
York State.  
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Addressing this overload will provide a reduction in constraints on the Western New 
York transmission system, allowing for the expansion of renewable generation imports.  
The increase in renewable generation availability will help to meet the renewable goals 
set for New York State looking forward to 2022, resulting in greater customer access to 
renewable energy.   
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative conductor types were analyzed for this project.  It was determined that the 
new conductor should match the previously installed conductor on Line 195 which shares 
the same double circuit structures. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Due to the 
timing of the need, it was determined that this project will not be evaluated for a potential 
NWA.    
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Load relief upgrades directly increase the maximum hosting capacity of the local EPS 
(electric power system) by two mechanisms. Increased asset capacity allows for a higher 
reverse power flow. Additionally, it allows more load to interconnect, which generally 
increases the threshold for certain higher cost interconnection upgrades (such as 3V0). 
This will enable PV and ESS to interconnect at higher volumes with a lower marginal 
interconnection cost. VVO directly contributes to system efficiency, contributing to EE 
targets, as well as reducing energy required from carbon heavy generation (by reducing 
the total energy procured from NYISO). Increasing efficiency also reduces peak loading, 
which may decrease the need for fossil fuel peaking plants. Transmission upgrades will 
eliminate congestions and allow for a more lower cost clean energy to reach load centers.

Program Name:

Associated Funding Numbers: C079506 - "Packard-Gardenville Reactors & 
Breakers"; C081799 - "Packard-Gardenville Reconfiguration” 
 
Description: 
 
This project reconfigures the 115kV Niagara-Gardenville Line 180, Packard-Gardenville 
182 and Packard-Gardenville 181-922 and retired-in-place Lines 91, 92 and 105.  First, 
Line 181-922 will be split into two sperate circuits and the right of way reconfigured.  
Between Ellicott Junction in the Town of Tonawanda and George Urban Blvd in 
Cheektowaga, place the 180 and 182 lines on the same structures, by swapping the 180 
and the retired in place 92 lines.  Between George Urban Blvd and Gardenville in West 
Seneca, reenergize three retired in place circuits.  The right of way between George 
Urban Blvd and Gardenville would be reconfigured to keep 180 and 182 on the same 
towers, put 181 and a retired in place circuit on the same tower and put a new line (922) 
on the same structures as line 54.  The 181 line would be reconfigured to connect 
between Packard and Gardenville.  The reconfigured Line 180 will connect between 
Niagara and Gardenville as a bussed line on double circuit towers.  The newly created 
line would connect Gardenville and Erie via the NYSEG owned section of the 922 line.  
Finally, the Packard – Gardenville 181 and 182 lines would both have 1% (4mH) series 
reactors installed at the Packard end of the lines.. The project will also the relocation of 
approximately 3 miles of 34.5kV Ludwig-Gardenville #704.

C079506, C081799 
Packard-Erie 181 Packard-Gardenville 182 
Overloads 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Packard – Erie 181 and Packard – Gardenville 182 lines are overloaded under certain 
system conditions and are a limiting factor for the amount of power imported from 
Ontario and generated within NY at the Niagara/Lewiston facility.  The overloads occur 
for N-1 outages of parallel facilities.  The maximum N-1 loading on these lines was 
201MVA (121% of the Long Term Emergency (LTE) rating) on Line 181 and 231MVA 
(111% of the LTE rating) on Line 182.  
 
The N-1 loading on these facilities for the design contingencies defined in Transmission 
Group Procedure 28 surpasses the LTE rating of the conductor.  Operating the lines 
within their rating would require reductions at the Niagara/Lewiston facility and 
reductions to the Ontario imports.  The limitations set by thermal ratings on these lines, 
constrain the initiative for increased clean energy in New York State. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Addressing these overloads will provide a reduction in constraints on the Western New 
York transmission system, allowing for the expansion of renewable generation imports.  
The increase in renewable generation availability will help to meet the renewable goals 
set for New York State looking forward to 2022, resulting in greater customer access to 
renewable energy.  
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Reconfigure and Reconductor NYSEG circuit:  Reconfigure the right of 
way between Ellicott Junction and George Urban Blvd to place the 180 and 182 lines on 
the same structures, by swapping the 180 and the retired in place 92 lines.  Bus the 181 
and the retired 92 line to create one circuit.  Reconductor NYSEG’s 922 line between the 
Urban Switch and Erie.  The bussed line will be renamed as the new line 180 between 
Niagara and Gardenville.  The previously named 180 will be renamed as line 181 
between Packard and Gardenville. 
 
Alternative 2 - Conductor Replacement and Reactor Alternative:  Replace 16.6 miles of 
conductor on line 181 and put a 4.3% series reactor on line 182 at Packard.   :  Conductor 
Replacement and Reactor Alternative:  Replace 16.6 miles of conductor on line 181 and 
put a 4.3% series reactor on line 182 at Packard.    
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the

Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Load relief upgrades directly increase the maximum hosting capacity of the local EPS 
(electric power system) by two mechanisms. Increased asset capacity allows for a higher 
reverse power flow. Additionally, it allows more load to interconnect, which generally 
increases the threshold for certain higher cost interconnection upgrades (such as 3V0). 
This will enable PV and ESS to interconnect at higher volumes with a lower marginal 
interconnection cost. VVO directly contributes to system efficiency, contributing to EE 
targets, as well as reducing energy required from carbon heavy generation (by reducing 
the total energy procured from NYISO). Increasing efficiency also reduces peak loading, 
which may decrease the need for Fossil Fuel peaking plants. Transmission upgrades will 
eliminate congestions and allow for a more lower cost clean energy to reach load centers.

Program Name: 
Component Fatigue/Deterioration 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project involves replacing 2,100 circuit feet of underground high-pressure oil filled 
pipe-type cables with solid dielectric cables for each of the 115kV Lockport-Mortimer 
#111, #113 and #114 transmission lines. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Rochester Pumping Plant pressurizes the three underground cables on the Lockport – 
Mortimer #111, #113, and #114 transmission lines. The underground circuits are installed 
in 10” steel pipes, each one about 0.4 miles long, starting at the West terminal and 
traverse beneath the Rochester Airport runway to the East terminal.  
The pumping plant has been in service since 1964 and although it underwent a 
refurbishment in 2004 after a pipe leak occurred on the #111 line, it is showing signs of 
deterioration that must be addressed to avoid future reliability issues.   Terminations at 
both ends of the cables are also nearing their expected end of life.   
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Using solid dielectric cables, instead of oil filled pipe-type cables, will remove the oil 
from the cable system and eliminate environmental concerns due to oil leaks. Solid 
dielectric cables are also less maintenance intensive compared to the high-pressure oil

Replace all terminations  
Life extension of 15yrs  
Higher whole wife costing over the period of 40yrs  
 
Alternative 3 - System Reconfiguration/Retire the Line 
 
This alternative is not feasible as these transmission lines are required to serve customers.

Description: 
 
This project will procure a 115kV, 30MVAR mobile capacitor bank that will be utilized 
as a stop gap measure at substations where a need for voltage support has been identified 
based on system studies until a permanent solution can be implemented, and for 
emergency situations. This mobile will be stored in the Western New York (WNY) 
region but can be utilized across Upstate NY. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
There are presently two (2) 115kV mobile capacitor banks in upstate NY, and both were 
recently placed in service to support project work.  This leaves the system without a 
mobile to address future contingencies.  The new mobile capacitor bank will reduce the 
likelihood of being without an available 115kV mobile capacitor bank when needed, and 
will reduce the average time and expense of deployment by ultimately allowing one 
mobile to be stored in each region.

capacitor bank.  The new 115kV 30MVAR mobile capacitor will allow for the access to

Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Reliability upgrades improve the system's ability to avoid a contingency (hardening, 
flood mitigation), reduce the exposure to contingency (fusing), and/or improve post 
contingency system capacity (MWh violation upgrades). Such benefits create more 
opportunities for renewable energy resources DER (such as PV and ESS) to export 
power, thereby improving the economics of individual projects. Further, improved 
reliability mitigates the need for load customers to operate backup generation, which is 
typically natural gas or petroleum fueled generation.

National Grid’s 115kV equipment while the lower yard is shared with Brookfield’s assets 
and contains all of the National Grid’s 34.5kV equipment. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The planned replacement of this substation reduces the likelihood of an in-service failure 
of deteriorated assets which can lead to long-term interruptions of the transmission 
system as well as customer outages.  
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - The replacement of the 34.5kV assets at the existing location, which 
includes ground grid for entire 34.5kV lower yard, four (4) 34.5kV OCB’s, one (1) 
overhead bus structure  and bus work,  two (2) surge arrestors, 34.5kV PT’s (Potential 
Transformers), and six (6) hot stick switches. 
 
Alternative 2 - The expansion of the 115kV upper yard fence to allow for installation of a 
new metalclad for the 34.5kV equipment, while leaving room for the 115kV equipment 
in the future. Extend the upper yard’s ground grid to allow for the new equipment. 
Replace TB#3 with a new 115kV-34.5kV 30/40/50 MVA transformer. Install eleven (11) 
PT’s, two (2) slip on CT’s (Current Transformers). The relocation of two(2) 34.5kV sub-
transmission lines due to the new location of the 34.5kV circuit breakers. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
As the project is driven by asset condition, it does not meet the NWA suitability criteria 
thresholds.

by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the 
governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by 
replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This on the Huntley-Lockport 36/37 Taps to Ayer Rd. project addresses the asset 
condition related issues 
 
The Huntley-Lockport 36/37 Taps to Ayer Rd are built overhead for 1.17 miles before 
transitioning underground for 2.5 miles to the Ayer Rd Station. There are (27) structures, 
and primarily uses 636 ACSR conductor. There is a single steel shield wire on each set of 
single circuit towers. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The overhead portion of the Huntley-Lockport 36/37 Taps to Ayer Rd are operating on 
Steel Lattice Towers from the former 25 cycle 92E and 92W circuits. These towers date 
to 1907. They are in poor condition and are in need of replacement. The foundations are 
in crumbling condition, and the steel shows significant oxidation.   
 
The 36/37 Ayer Road taps supply a significant number of customers. Both taps supply 
the Ayer Rd Distribution station and have 4,844 customers at risk.

C081676 
Spier-Rotterdam 2 Re-insulate (Phase 2) 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Conductor Clearance: Scheduled FY21 
 
The scope of this asset condition refurbishment project includes a full aerial 
comprehensive inspection including UV and corona, steel tower climbing inspection, and 
Osmose PIT inspection for the wood. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
This project is the second phase of the Spier-Rotterdam #2 asset condition refurbishment. 
This circuit still has insulators and hardware from the original line installation. There 
have been spot replacements when equipment has failed on this line, but a total 
refurbishment has not been completed. Age is not a determining factor for asset 
replacement, however age is a factor when ranking circuits for evaluation.  The earliest 
records found in PowerPlant indicate this Major Location still has 245 structures installed 
in 1923. 
 
In the past five (5) years this line has had 12 operations: 10 being momentary and two (2) 
being lockouts. All but one (1) of these events have been attributed to unknown causes. 
Additionally, from Str. 178 to Rotterdam we have found instances of the 397.5 MCM 
24/7 ACSS conductor bird caging. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to provide reliable service to customers served by 
National Grid.  This overhead line refurbishment program promotes safety and reliability 
by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the 
governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by 
replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
The following alternatives will be considered as part of the Needs Case pending 
inspection: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Refurbishment: This alternative replaces deteriorated structures, 
insulators and hardware, adds improved grounding, and targeted replacement of 
conductor and shield wire on the mainline and taps, 
 
Alternative 2 - Line Rebuild: If the conductor fails testing and it is deemed the steel 
structures are too deteriorated to remain in service, the circuit will need to be rebuilt,

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program - Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers: C081750, C034193, C077024 
 
Description: 
 
The refurbishment of the double circuit 115kV Gardenville-Dunkirk #141/#142 was 
originally conceived as a 44.96 mile refurbishment to address all structures, conductor, 
and shield wire.  However, due to the real estate challenges in the Villages of Angola and 
Silver Creek including the need to move the line off of the present alignment in those 
villages, it was broken down into Northern and Southern phases.   The Southern Phase 
addresses assets between North Angola substation and Dunkirk substation including 
those assets in the Villages of Angola and Silver Creek.   
 
The southern portion entails a full rebuild utilizing approximately 14 miles of the 230kV 
Gardenville-Dunkirk Corridor that is further in-land from Lake Erie.   Near existing 
structure 444, the new alignment meets the existing Right -of-Way where the rebuild will 
occur on the existing alignment south to Dunkirk.  When completed, the mainline will be 
approximately 26.4 miles and a new Tap to NYSEG Silver Creek Station will be created.  
Part of the tap to NYSEG Silver Creek substation will be on the existing alignment.  The 
rebuild will utilize 795kcmil ACSR “Drake” conductor with one steel shield wire and one 
OPGW.  Approximately 4 miles of new right-of-way will be required.  The sections of 
Line between approximately North Angola substation and just south of Irving will be 
removed. The sections of line between NYSEG Silver Creek substation to approximately 
the NYS Thruway (I-90) will also be removed. 
 
C034193 is a separate project that represents the segment of line that travels through land

owned by the Seneca Nation of Indians. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The 141/142 was placed in-service initially in 1920 with 341 steel structures.  In the years 
since, additional structures both steel and wood were added.  The 141/142 serves a total 
of 20,000 National Grid customers.  The segment south of the North Angola Substation 
contains the NYSEG Silver Creek Substation and the National Grid Dunkirk Substation.  
The Dunkirk Substation is a transmission substation that has 230kV, 115kV, and 34.5kV. 
 
The steel assets on the 141/142 were placed in-service in 1920 and have not received the 
recommended 20-year cycle for painting.   Structural steel members supporting the arms 
are light angle sections that show from aerial photographs corrosion at and near the 
bolted connections.  This thinning of the steel section reduces the strength of the arm. 
 
As part of the steel structure condition assessment for both phases of the project, the 
structures were inspected from the air and a shakedown inspection was also performed by 
a contract journeyman linemen firm.  These inspections were used to identify visual 
defects that may not have been identified by traditional ground based or aerial 
inspections. 
 
The Southern Phase is approximately 25 miles encompassing from the North Angola 
Substation (Tower#249) to the Dunkirk Substation (Tower#581).  It contains 
predominantly 4/0 ACSR 6/1 Penguin with a section of 636.0 kcmil AAC 37 strand 
Orchid conductor at the Dunkirk end.  The Northern Phase is being reconductored with 
795 kcmil ACSR Drake. The National Grid Worcester Laboratory performed tensile 
strength, torsion tests, and corrosion analysis on a total of five (5) conductor samples in 
2011 to support the reconductoring of the 141/142. 
 
The 4/0 ACSR had a calculated breaking strength 2.73% less than the rated breaking 
strength and marginally passed the torsion test and passed the corrosion analysis that 
looks at the amount of residual zinc on the steel core strand.  The 636.0 kcmil AAC was 
only tested for tension and those samples passed by 6.71% over rated breaking strength. 
 
Transmission Planning supports a project that replaces the 4/0 ACSR with a larger 
conductor.  The 4/0 ACSR is marginal for some of the load cases and with the Northern 
Phase being reconductored with 795kcmil ACSR, the Southern Phase also requires 
reconductoring with a similar ampacity conductor to realize full capacity from 
Gardenville to Dunkirk. 
The Line 141/142 southern portion currently routes overhead through the Village of 
Angola and Village of Silver Creek. Alternatives to re-route the line from passing over 
residential homes in these villages is included in the scope of work.

Between 6/3/2012 and 3/1/2018 the 141/142 sustained (45) total faults of which (16) 
faults were unknown cause. It has not been confirmed that the polymer insulators were 
the cause; but with the UV/corona inspection yielding leaking current, there is strong 
evidence.  On the day of the UV inspection none of the porcelain insulators were 
identified to be tracking.  However past aerial visual inspections have noted a large 
percentage of porcelain insulators exhibited evidence of flashover.  
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Reconductoring with a larger conductor will provide additional capacity for using during 
contingencies and to support the additional renewable energy resources being able to 
participate in the market.  . This will additional capacity will also improve resiliency. 
 
Public safety is a driver of this project as well. Removing the energized 141/142 from 
passing over occupied residences and hardening the 141/142 at critical road crossings 
will improve safety.

Alternative 2 - For this option the existing assets would be replaced with a combination

Alternative 3 - For this option, starting just north of North Angola Substation, 1.85 miles 
of new double circuit 115kV will be constructed south-east to the existing 230kV 
corridor. The new circuit will be a combination of steel poles on concrete foundations for 
the dead-ends and direct-embedded steel poles with steel davit arms for the tangents. The

Description: 
 
The replacement of deteriorated 115kV and 23kV assets including  twenty-seven (27) 
115kV bus insulators, six (6) 115kV surge arresters, one (1) 115kV – 23kV 
20/26/33MVA power transformer, four (4) 23kV Oil Circuit Breakers (OCBs), one (1) 
23kV Station Service Transformer, twenty-one (21) bus supports and eighteen (18) surge 
arrestors.  In addition, there will be a  separation of assets from Brookfield Power and 
National Grid at the shared facility.  A new control house will be installed with IEC-
61850 communication protocol, and a emergency generator.   
 
Project Justification: 
 
The Taylorville Substation is a shared facility between National Grid and Brookfield 
Renewable Power. The protection, controls and communication equipment for National 
Grid’s yard assets are located within the Brookfield owned Powerhouse.  The substation 
yard is combined with Brookfield’s owned 23kV assets and the step-up power 
transformer.   
 
The 115kV circuit breaker assets were replaced in 1991 and are in good condition and are 
in a straight bus configuration with a tie-breaker.  There are six (6) 115kV transmission 
lines at the substation and there five (5)  23kV Sub-transmission lines at the substation.  
There is one (1) 115kV – 23kV Transformer #2 (TR#2) that was manufactured by

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  NA 
 
Description: 
 
This project provides for the rebuild of the Dewitt 115kV station to meet NPCC 
Directory 4 requirements.  NPCC Directory 4 requires independent batteries or elements 
for each of the independent protection systems.  It is anticipated that a bay-by-bay rebuild 
will occur with two independent protection systems and batteries/elements.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
NPCC Task Forces have been working on a revised A10 document, which is the 
methodology for the classification of Bulk Power System (BPS) stations and elements.  
During the work on this revised document, preliminary testing was done by the NYISO 
to determine if the proposed changes to the testing strategy would impact the 
classification of any NY stations.  In one scenario, the Dewitt 115kV bus was found to 
test positive as BPS.  Final determination of the BPS status of Dewitt is expected in late 
calendar year 2020.  If the station is classified as BPS, upgrades will be necessary to 
bring the station into compliance with the NPCC Directory 4 protection requirements

This project would maintain compliance with NPCC Directory 4 requirements.  The goal

security of the interconnected system in the Northeast United States 
 
Alternatives: 
 
No alternatives exist as compliance with the NPCC criteria is mandatory.   
 
DER/NWA Alternative:   
 
This project is required to compliance with NPCC Directory 4 requirements. This need 
cannot be met by an NWA Alternative. 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Load relief upgrades directly increase the maximum hosting capacity of the local EPS 
(electric power system) by two mechanisms. Increased asset capacity allows for a higher 
reverse power flow. Additionally, it allows more load to interconnect, which generally 
increases the threshold for certain higher cost interconnection upgrades (such as 3V0). 
This will enable PV and ESS to interconnect at higher volumes with a lower marginal 
interconnection cost. VVO directly contributes to system efficiency, contributing to EE 
targets, as well as reducing energy required from carbon heavy generation (by reducing 
the total energy procured from NYISO). Increasing efficiency also reduces peak loading, 
which may decrease the need for Fossil Fuel peaking plants. Transmission upgrades will 
eliminate congestions and allow for a more lower cost clean energy to reach load centers.

23kV, and 13.2kV voltages.  
 
There are four (4) 115kV circuits connected at the station, four (4) transformers with two 
(2) going to the 23kV and two (2) going to the 13.2kV yards, six (6) 13.2kV feeders and 
two (2) overhead 23kV circuits. The substation was installed in 1959. 
 
The 115kV bus is presently designed as straight bus without a tie-circuit breaker.  This 
creates operational concern. 
 
There two (2) 115kV – 23kV, 15/20/25MVA Transformers #1 (TR#1) and #2 (TR#2).  
The TR#1 was manufactured by General Electric in 1959 and TR#2 was manufactured by 
Moloney Electric in 1959 and both have deteriorated and a history of leaks.  The TR#2 
also has limited spare parts and no Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) support. 
 
The 115kV circuit switcher R1710 manufactured by S&C in 1987 and designed for the 
capacitor.  Presently it has over 6000 operations this is more than the recommended 
operations and usage by the manufacturer S&C.    
 
The twelve (12) 115kV single phase hook stick type disconnects are original to the 
substation and are in deteriorated condition.  Similar disconnects at the substation have 
already been replaced due to asset condition and cracked insulators. 
 
The two (2) 115kV gang-operated disconnects are original to the substation and are in 
deteriorated condition.  Similar disconnects at the substation have already been replaced 
due to asset condition and cracked insulators. 
 
The six (6) 115kV Oil filled VTs are manufactured by ABB in 1993.  These VTs have

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
Projects to enhance Regional Control Center Operations through the implementation of a 
dedicated Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system along with a 
Digital Management System (DMS) requires the expansion of Remote Terminal Units 
(RTUs) in the Company’s substations and the reconfiguration of some RTUs that are 
managing both transmission and distribution assets. 
 
This project supports control center capabilities by installing and reconfiguring RTUs in 
substations in which the control and monitoring of T&D assets utilize a common RTU. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Increasing volumes of distribution assets to be monitored and controlled, both Company 
assets and those of Distribution Energy Resources (DERs) providers, is driving the need 
to expand the capabilities of the SCADA system. The proliferation of distributed 
intelligent devices in support of distribution system operations also increases cyber 
security risks. As part of this expansion the Company proposes to separate T&D SCADA 
systems to improve database performance and enhance cyber security and NERC CIP 
protections related to the Bulk Electric System (BES).

Customer Benefit: 
 
This program provides a means to enhance the situational awareness of distribution

Alternatives: 
 
Do Nothing - This is not recommended since to continue to operate with the present 
SCADA would maintain the existing system and not enhance the network to be readily 
connect possible DER integrations. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA. Based on the 
Company’s evaluation, the need addressed by this project does not satisfy one or more 
element of the Suitability Criteria and will not be evaluated for a potential NWA. 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
The replacement of obsolete equipment and expanding the Company’s communication 
network capability will provide a communication backbone for numerous grid 
modernization functions.  Communication and Control programs directly improve the 
Company's ability to efficiently interconnect and operate DER. These technologies 
enable lower cost interconnections by allowing the Company to explore techniques such 
as flexible interconnection and advanced dispatch for programs like NWA. Telecom and 
Control (consistency in name of program) will enable more PV and ESS to interconnect 
to the system more efficiently. EMS / SCADA gives the company higher visibility into 
system conditions, allowing planners to make fewer assumptions, and be less 
conservative when interconnecting DG. This may lead to higher penetration of DG at 
lower costs.

Description: 
 
Add a second 115-69kV transformer at Rotterdam, along with a high-side 115kV circuit 
switcher to increase capacity and resiliency. Additionally, rebuild the Rotterdam 69kV 
yard to 115kV standards to address asset condition concerns and allow for a new bus 
configuration, wherein each of the two 69kV lines is connected via a breaker and bus 
section to a separate 115-69kV transformer to alleviate post-contingency overloading. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Between 2017 and 2019, a combined 700MW of solar generation was proposed on the 
transmission, sub transmission, and distribution networks in the Mohawk Valley. The 
existing system does not have the capacity to deliver all of the proposed generation in 
real-time. Production cost modelling found that constraints within the local transmission 
networks that would result in an estimated 136GWh of annual curtailment. Increasing the 
capacity of the most binding transmission elements is expected to unbottle 115GWh 
annually of curtailed generation. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
This project will allow for increased real-time deliverability of renewable resources, 
progressing toward the state's clean energy goals and bringing down the cost of energy

Alternatives:

Finally, the use of two transformers provides for greater system resiliency over the use of 
a single transformer.

New York State looking forward to 2022, resulting in greater customer access to 
renewable energy.

justification for this project is MVT, it was determined that this project will not be 
evaluated for a potential NWA.

Program Name:

Associated Funding Numbers: 
 
C082190: Indian River-Lyme Junction Line. C082192: Indian River-Lyme Junction 
Station. C082202: Indian River-Lyme Junction Land. C084534: Coffeen Bus Tie 
 
Description: 
 
These projects build 8.6 miles of 336.4 kcmil ACSR 26/7 transmission line from Indian 
River station to Lyme Tap. They also expand the 115kV bus and add breaker to Indian 
River Station for the new 115kV line to Lyme Tap. Furthermore, a new four breaker ring 
bus station at Lyme Tap will be built.  The Coffeen substation 115kV bus is also split into 
two bus sections 
 
Project Justification: 
 
A single line outage of the radial Thousand Island – Coffeen circuit interrupts 16,600 
customers.  A single line outage of the radial Coffeen – West Adams line interrupts 9,500 
customers.  A bus fault at Coffeen interrupts both radial lines impacting 26,100 
customers as well as the 7100 Customers served directly off the Coffeen bus.  A single 
line outage of the radial Fort Drum – Black River line interrupts 6,000 customers.  An N-
2 outage of both circuits serving Coffeen station results in an outage to both radial lines 
out of Coffeen and the stations served from those lines for 32,800 customers total.

C082190, C082192, C082202 
115 kV Indian River-Lyme Junction New

The operability of the area is significantly improved by reducing the number of 
conditions that can lead to customer outages.  This is achieved by breaking the Thousand 
Island – Coffeen circuit into three lines, eliminating the Coffeen bus fault and eliminating 
the radial nature of the Fort Drum – Black River circuit.  Segmenting the line will also 
result in faster identification of the fault location which would lead to faster restoration of 
customers.   
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Beyond lowering the probability of an outage occurring the maximum number of 
customers interrupted for a single line outage will be reduced from 16,600 to 9,500 and 
the number of customers interrupted for an outage of two circuits will be reduced from 
32,800 to no more than 16,600.  However, many of the N-2 conditions that result in 
customer outages today will be eliminated.  
 
Interruption estimates from US Department of Energy, (ICE) Calculator, were used to 
estimate customer power outage costs. Due to the higher risk of severe storms in this 
area, two 24 hour outages were assumed to occur to the customers served from these lines 
over the 50 year life of the assets, which would have a cost of $58.6M. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Do nothing and continue to accept the outage exposure.  
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Since the 
justification for this project is resiliency, it was determined that this project will not be 
evaluated for a potential NWA.

Program Name: 
Smart Fault Indicator Program-NY 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
The program will install smart fault indicators on the 115kv transmission system. Each 
year, the Transmission Asset Management group and the Transmission Control Center 
will identify and select circuits that will benefit from the installation of these smart fault 
indicators based on the worst performing circuits list, past reliability data and any current 
needs.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
Smart fault indicators are a useful tool for utilities. When a fault occurs on the system, 
field personal are sent to patrol the line to identify any issues before repairs can be made 
and the line can be restored. Currently, National Grid uses fault indicators that do not 
communicate with any of our systems and have to be viewed in the field to determine 
their reading. With the advancements of technology, we now have access to smart fault 
indicators which are tied into the companies systems and can be viewed remotely. This 
allows the company to more accurately dispatch field personal, expedite switching 
operations, decrease the length of patrol for field personnel and ultimately reduces 
restoration times.  
 
 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 287 of 371


--- Page 438 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 288 of 371 
C082281 
Smart Fault Indicator Program-NY 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The main benefit of this program is reduced outage times. Crews are dispatched closer to 
the fault location, have less line to patrol, switching operations are streamlined, and the 
transmission control center can get the full picture without having to send a crew to check 
each set of indicators in the field. In addition, these indicators can be used to narrow 
down the location of momentary operations. This has the benefit of reducing costs for 
patrols and inspections and minimizes the chances of fixing assets that are not faulty. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
The alternative to this program would be to continue installing fault indicators with no 
smart capabilities. This would not improve outage times and is not recommended. 
Technology has improved and these indicators with no communication capabilities are 
outdated equipment. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative:   
 
Due to the driver of this project being asset condition it does not satisfy the NWA 
suitability criteria.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project replaces the (20) failed/failing culverts between Omphalius Road and Sharp 
Road under the 151/152 Gardenville-Five Mile Road Corridor using the most economical 
and feasible design/method listed below: 
 
• Replacement with a 3-Sided Box/Mod Block Culvert 
• Replacement with a ConSpan Culvert 
• Replacement with a Reinforced Concrete Pipe 
• Replace by utilizing Bore/Micro-Tunnel Pipe 
• Utilize Spray Reinforcement on existing culvert 
• Remove the existing culvert, grade slopes down and install Armor on an 
uncovered stream 
Project Justification: 
 
During the Fall 2018, Transmission Maintenance was notified by a landowner of a slope 
failure in the 151/152 Gardenville-Five Mile Rd corridor just north of Abbott Hill Rd, in 
the Town of Concord.  Following a site visit and subsequent comprehensive inspection of 
the corridor from the air numerous other areas were identified.   
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 290 of 371


--- Page 441 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 291 of 371 
C082708 
151/152 Gardenville-Five Mile Rd Culvert 
Erosion Damage/Failure 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
The travel path on top of the embankment at this location is too narrow for vehicles to 
traverse down the right of way.  Fortunately, at this time no 115kV double circuit 
transmission structures are in imminent danger.  However, slope stability and culvert 
deterioration needs to be remediated so land owner property, access roads and electric 
assets are not damaged.  
 
Fisher Associates, a civil and environmental consulting engineering firm, were retained 
to inspect the corridor and triage sites that required immediate attention from those that 
could be repaired/replaced later.  It was determined by Fisher and confirmed by National 
Grid that (20) of the (108) culverts under the 151/152 Gardenville-Five Mile Rd corridor 
between Str 127 at the north end at Omphalius Road and Str 208 at the south end south of 
Sharp Road were in immediate need of replacement.   
 
Currently with the culverts and wing walls failing or failed, fine-grained soils are mixing 
with storm water and potentially reaching Eighteen Mile Creek which is a NYSDEC 
Class A, A stream. If a culvert fails, allowing turbidity to reach Eighteen Mile Creek, 
National Grid could suffer severe reputational consequences. 
 
Fisher Associates has inspected all (108) culverts, and identified (20) culverts as urgent in 
nature. The recommendation is to address these culverts as soon as possible.  
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The community should be supportive of this project as many of them over the past few 
years have been affected by flooding caused by inadequately sized or plugged culverts.  
 
The community would benefit from the conservation of a clean Eighteen Mile Creek. 
This ensures that fish and wildlife are undisrupted from a failure of a culvert. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Replace the (20) failed/failing culverts using the most economical and feasible 
design/method listed below: 
 
• Replacement with a 3-Sided Box/Mod Block Culvert 
• Replacement with a ConSpan Culvert 
• Replacement with a Reinforced Concrete Pipe 
• Replace by utilizing Bore/Micro-Tunnel Pipe 
• Utilize Spray Reinforcement on existing culvert

Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Reliability upgrades improve the system's ability to avoid a contingency (hardening, 
flood mitigation), reduce the exposure to contingency (fusing), and/or improve post 
contingency system capacity (MWh violation upgrades). Such benefits create more 
opportunities for renewable energy resources DER (such as PV and ESS) to export 
power, thereby improving the economics of individual projects. Further, improved 
reliability mitigates the need for load customers to operate backup generation, which is 
typically natural gas or petroleum fueled generation.

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program – Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  C039521 
 
Description: 
 
The project is to advance construction of two off-corridor access roads to access the five 
structures atop Mount Defiance.  As of February 2019, all easements have been secured.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
The 115kV Ticonderoga-Whitehall #3 was placed in-service in 1930 and is a radially fed 
circuit from Whitehall.  It connects electrically to the radial 115kV Ticonderoga-Republic 
#2.  The Mount Defiance section of the circuit is defined as Str. 447 to Str. 453.  Access 
to Str. 448 - Str. 452 is not possible via conventional means, due to the presence of 
several near vertical rock faces.  The only access is off corridor from privately owned 
lands; and that access is limited to foot paths that will not accommodate motor vehicles 
of any kind.  
 
The structures on Mt. Defiance have been the topic of numerous past projects that were 
ultimately rejected due to problems associated with terrain; steep (near vertical) slopes 
with exposed bedrock, lack of on corridor access, small customer base, and difficulty 
taking outages required for construction due to the radial nature of the line. 
An outage on the Ticonderoga-Republic #2 line will interrupt approximately 10,000 
customers and up to 33.84 MVA of load (based on 2017 peak). The additional benefit of 
this project is to provide International Paper in Ticonderoga, the largest employer in the

Version 1 –

area, with reliable energy.  International Paper Ticonderoga has on-site generation but is 
unable to ride through a long-term outage.  IP needs the NMPC 115kV transmission 
circuit to ensure full operations. 
 
Age is not a determining factor for asset replacement.  However, the wood poles installed 
in the early 1930 do not have the same safety factors and strength contingencies as wood 
structures used today.  In addition, Str. 448 to 452 require hardening  as if these structures 
were to fail today, Ticonderoga and all points north would be without electricity for days 
or even weeks according to National Grid's transmission line department.  A prolonged 
outage would also have negative impacts on CAIDI (duration) reliability results. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The customer benefit to this project is the improved reliability of the sole source of power 
to National Grid's service territory in the northern Adirondack region. This stretch of our 
115kv system poses many access challenges and would considerably delay our 
restoration times if we were to encounter an issue.  Once access is created, the existing 
structures can be accessed using conventional means and methods. Our customers expect 
reliable service and this project will ensure we are able to deliver. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - If a structure or structures were to fail, replace them aerially using 
helicopters. As construction of emergency access would be too timely. 
 
Alternative 2 - Do nothing: This is not recommended as the existing wood pole structures 
date back to the early 1930's. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative:   
 
Due to the driver of this project being asset condition it does not satisfy the NWA 
suitability Criteria.  
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA): N/A

Program Name:  
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program – Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
Replace the wooden structures between structure number 24 through structure number 42 
on the Coffeen - Black River #3 circuit with direct-embedded steel pole H-Frames. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
In 2019 while performing maintenance work around structure numbers 28 through 42 on 
the Coffeen - Black River #3 115kV circuit, Transmission Line Services (TLS) found that 
this area showed signs of heavy woodpecker activity. With the notable exception of 
structure number 36 1/2, the structures in this section are wood. In 2011, Osmose 
inspected this circuit and found that all the poles were non-rejects. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Improving the asset health of the system, will reduce the likelihood of structure failures, 
which improves the reliability to our customers. Using steel in an area with known 
woodpecker active prevents the structures from being damaged from woodpeckers in the 
future.

Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to provide reliable service to customers served by 
National Grid.  This overhead line refurbishment program promotes safety and reliability 
by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the 
governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by 
replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
The following alternatives will be considered as part of the Needs Assessment  pending 
inspection: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Refurbishment: This alternative replaces deteriorated structures, 
insulators and hardware, adds improved grounding, and targeted replacement of 
conductor and shield wire on the mainline and taps, 
 
Alternative 2 - Line Rebuild: If the conductor fails testing and it is deemed the steel 
structures are too deteriorated to remain in service, the circuit will need to be rebuilt, 
 
Alternative 3 - Smart Fault Detection and Automated Line Switching:  This is an option 
to aid in restoring customers during a lockout but will not prevent customers from 
experiencing momentary interruptions.  
 
Alternative 4 - EV solutions: Cannot be implemented as these assets are still necessary to 
support the transmission system. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
As the project need  is driven by asset condition, it does not meet the NWA suitability 
criteria thresholds.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project rebuilds approximately 2.94mi of double-circuit 115kV Inghams-St 
Johnsville 6/Inghams-Richfield Springs 7-942 from Inghams Station to Structure 28 with 
1113 MCM ACSR 54/19 (or equivalent) conductor with new structures and hardware to 
increase capacity and address asset condition issues. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Between 2017 and 2019, a combined 700MW of solar generation was proposed on the 
transmission, sub transmission, and distribution networks in the Mohawk Valley. The 
existing system does not have the capacity to deliver all of the proposed generation in 
real-time. The 69kV system was built circa 1930 and has had occasional structure 
replacements from time to time.  Production cost modelling found that constraints within 
the local transmission networks that would result in an estimated 136GWh of annual 
curtailment. Increasing the capacity of the most binding transmission elements is 
expected to unbottle 115GWh annually of curtailed generation. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
This project will allow for increased real-time deliverability of renewable resources, 
progressing toward the state's clean energy goals and bringing down the cost of energy

the reliability of the local transmission system. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Curtail generation to secure the system. A hybrid conductor with an equivalent rating to 
1113 ACSR 54/19 was considered for reconductoring only, but was found to exceed 
double the weight of the presumed designed structure capacity of 4/0 Cu. Thus, it is 
likely that the combination of asset condition and the required conductor size would lead 
to significant, if not full, structure replacements. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Since the 
justification for this project is MVT (partially driven by Asset Condition), it was 
determined that this project will not be evaluated for a potential NWA.      
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
MultiValue Transmission projects unbottle clean energy. These projects enable clean 
generation (primarily solar and wind ) to delivery more clean energy to the bulk system, 
directly supporting several CLCPA targets.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
Add remote control capability to the existing 115kV switches 522 and 511 outside 
Boyntonville on the North Troy - Hoosick #5. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
An outage of the North Troy - Hoosick circuit interrupts 5,300 customers at 
Boyntonville.  The remoteness of this station and difficultly accessing the transmission 
line results in delays identifying the fault locations and thus long restoration times.  
Following a line outage, the switches can be used to isolate the faulted section of the line 
and restore customers.  With the possible location of the fault narrowed down to a smaller 
section of the lines it will be possible to identify and rectify the problem area quicker 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Customers at Boyntonville will see an improvement in the duration of interruptions.  
Interruption estimates from US Department of Energy, (ICE) Calculator, were used to 
estimate customer power outage costs.  One 24 hour outage was assumed to occur to the 
customers at this station over the 50 year life of the assets.

N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
Move the 6.7 mile long Duguid station tap off the 16 mile long Dewitt - Tilden line and 
connect it directly to the Dewitt station bus, creating a new line.   
 
Project Justification: 
 
An outage of the Clay – Dewitt #5 line results in a sustained outage to 9,500 customers 
and a momentary outage to 1,500 customers.  By spitting the Clay – Dewitt line into two 
lines, the overhead line exposure to a fault is reduced for customers served from both 
circuits.  The accuracy of distance to fault calculations will also be improved, which will 
result in faster identification of the fault location 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Interruption estimates from US Department of Energy, (ICE) Calculator, were used to 
estimate customer power outage costs.  One 24 hour outage was assumed to occur to the 
customers served from this line over the 50 year life of the assets.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project installs in-line breakers to each of the Huntley - Lockport (#36 and #37) 
lines to split them into a north and south section on the Huntley side of the Getzville 
transformers (TR1 & TR2).  This project also moves the tap connections to Ayer Road 
211 and Renaissance Drive 229 substations to the Huntley side of the new Getzville 
breakers to balance the customer exposure between each line section. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
An outage of both of the Huntley – Lockport 36 and 37 lines interrupts 33,000 customers.  
With the lines split into a North and South circuit, the number of customers interrupted 
by an outage of any two lines will be reduced from 33,000 customers to 18,100.  By 
splitting the circuits, the possible location of the fault will be narrowed down to a smaller 
section of each line which will result in faster identification and correction of the fault 
location. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Interruption estimates from US Department of Energy, (ICE) Calculator, were used to 
estimate customer power outage costs.  One 24 hour outage was assumed to occur to the 
customers served from these lines over the 50 year life of the assets.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project installs  an Automatic Line Sectionalizing (ALS) scheme at Whitaker 
(Switches 44 & 43) and Gilbert Mills (Switches 44 & 43) utilizing the existing 115kV 
switches. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
An outage of this 34 mile long circuit interrupts 5,700 customers served from Whitaker 
Station, 4,100 customers served from Gilbert Mills Station, plus 3 large industrial 
customers and a 115/34.5kV supply at Bristol Hill.  Following a line outage, the ALS will 
isolate the faulted section of the line and restore all customers at Whitaker and Gilbert 
Mills and depending on the fault location may also restore the industrial customers.  With 
the possible location of the fault narrowed down to a smaller section of the line it will be 
possible to identify and rectify the problem area quicker 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Customers served from this line will see an improvement in the number and duration of 
interruptions.  Interruption estimates from US Department of Energy, (ICE) Calculator, 
were used to estimate customer power outage costs.  One 24 hour outage was assumed to 
occur to the customers at these stations over the 50 year life of the assets.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
Install a Phase Angle Regulator (PAR) and associated equipment at Malone station on the 
Malone - Willis #1-910 115kV circuit. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Installation of the PAR will allow System Operators to control the flow of power between 
the 230kV system at Willis and the 115kV network.  The 115kV system from Malone to 
Colton and then south from Colton to Browns Falls, Taylorville and Boonville is heavily 
loaded and does constrain market operations.  Because of the difficulties securing these 
lines through local actions, the circuits have been added to the short list of 115kV 
facilities that are included in the NYISO day ahead scheduling software.  
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The PAR will increase the flexibility of the system and allow more efficient market 
operations.  Without the PAR, securing the local 115kV system often requires either 
National Grid or NYISO System Operators to curtail hydro or wind generation.  Thus, the 
PAR will increase the deliverability of renewable generation. 
 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 331 of 371

Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 332 of 371 
C084542 
Malone PAR 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Do nothing and continue to secure the system using curtailment of renewable generation.  
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
An NWA Alternative cannot meet the need (redirection of powerflow) met by this PAR 
project. 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Load relief upgrades directly increase the maximum hosting capacity of the local EPS 
(electric power system) by two mechanisms. Increased asset capacity allows for a higher 
reverse power flow. Additionally, it allows more load to interconnect, which generally 
increases the threshold for certain higher cost interconnection upgrades (such as 3V0). 
This will enable PV and ESS to interconnect at higher volumes with a lower marginal 
interconnection cost. VVO directly contributes to system efficiency, contributing to EE 
targets, as well as reducing energy required from carbon heavy generation (by reducing 
the total energy procured from NYISO). Increasing efficiency also reduces peak loading, 
which may decrease the need for fossil fuel peaking plants. Transmission upgrades will 
eliminate congestions and allow for a more lower cost clean energy to reach load centers.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project installs an Automatic Line Sectionalizing (ALS) scheme at New Krumkill 
utilizing existing 115kV motor-operated disconnects MOD 788 and MOD 888. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Loss of the circuit between Albany and the CEST station interrupts the Mckownville and 
New Krumkill stations. The Mckownville station has an Automatic Line Sectionalizing 
(ALS) scheme that will restore customers at that station to service once the fault has 
cleared.  However, the 6,800 customers at New Krumkill may not be restored depending 
on the location of the fault.  Following a line outage, the ALS will isolate the faulted 
section of the line and restore customers.  With the possible location of the fault narrowed 
down to a smaller section of the line it will be possible to identify and rectify the problem 
area quicker 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Customers at New Krumkill will see an improvement in the duration of interruptions.  
Interruption estimates from US Department of Energy, (ICE) Calculator, were used to 
estimate customer power outage costs.  One 24 hour outage was assumed to occur to the 
customers at New Krumkill over the 50 year life of the assets.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
Replace 3 overdutied breakers.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
Energy Highway Project Segment A and B projects will increase fault duty in the area. 
The breakers at Leeds will exceed their interrupting duty and need to be replaced to 
handle the increase in fault current. Duty in excess of a breaker's nameplate capability 
indicates a potential for catastrophic failure if a breaker is exposed to the associated 
worst-case fault. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Replacing breakers with higher interrupting capability will allow the breakers to safely 
interrupt and withstand faults. This will increase transmission system reliability, mitigate 
the risks of unwanted outages, safety and environmental concerns associated with 
equipment failure.

generation resources. 
 
Customer Benefit:

cost of energy.  The project would also mitigate a possible adverse impact if the 
Generator were to decide to retire.

C084553 
Worst Performing Circuits 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Type: 
 
T SubT D 
X 
 
 
 
 
Spending Rationale: 
Asset Condition 
Communications/ 
Control Systems 
Customer 
Requests/ Public 
Requirements 
DER Electric 
System 
Access 
Damage/ Failure

Infrastructure 
Reliability 
Resiliency 
System 
Capacity 
Multi-Value 
Transmission 
(MVT) 
  
X 
  
  
  
 
 
Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This program will address the worst performing 115kV circuits across New York State. 
The rankings are based on five (5) year non-storm data and are targeted on the impact to 
our customers. These rankings are run once a year in order to catch new poor performers 
and to remove circuits that have been addressed during the prior year. Each year the top 
20 circuits are identified along with the primary performance driver for each circuit. This 
driver can range from lightning strikes to failed line equipment to wind events. Various 
inspections and patrols are preformed to identify the deficiencies that are causing these 
primary drivers. An improvement plan is then formulated to address the deficiencies. 
 
Project Justification: 
 
The primary goal of this program is to address reliability concerns on the 115kV system 
across New York State. The circuits identified have the biggest impacts to our customers 
in both total SAIFI and lost customer minutes. For FY20, the top 20 circuits account for 
66% of non-storm SAIFI-T and 64% of the total lost customer minutes. By fixing the 
issues on these circuits we will be increasing the reliability to the customers most affected 
by the reliability of the 115kV system. 
 
 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 348 of 371


--- Page 499 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 349 of 371 
C084553 
Worst Performing Circuits 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
The customer benefit to this program is better reliability on the 115kV lines that were the 
worst performers from the prior five (5) years. This means that we will be investing the 
rate payers money directly into the lines that impact customer reliability the most. These 
lines feed both large industrial customers as well as the substations that then feed our 
distribution systems and provide service to residential and commercial customers. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
Alternative 1 - Replace assets when lines are refurbished, or failures occur. 
 
Alternative 2 - NWA/REV solutions: Cannot be implemented as these assets are still 
necessary to support the transmission system. 
 
DER/NWA Alternative:   
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Since this is 
a program, and not a specific project, it was determined that this project will not be 
evaluated for a potential NWA 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Reliability upgrades improve the system's ability to avoid a contingency (hardening, 
flood mitigation), reduce the exposure to contingency (fusing), and/or improve post 
contingency system capacity (MWh violation upgrades). Such benefits create more 
opportunities for renewable energy resources DER (such as PV and ESS) to export 
power, thereby improving the economics of individual projects. Further, improved 
reliability mitigates the need for load customers to operate backup generation, which is 
typically natural gas or petroleum fueled generation.

Program Name: 
Overhead Line Refurbishment Program – Asset Condition 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
This project will address asset condition related issues on the 115kV New Scotland-Feura 
Bush #9 (T5500) and The New Scotland-Long Lane #7 (T5470). These two circuits are 
primarily run on joint steel structures and wood poles. The overhead line details follow: 
 
Total length: 4.16 miles (T5470) / 4.03 (T5500) 
Conductor Types: 795 MCM ACSR, 4/0 7S CU, 336.4 MCM 
Total number of structures: 68 
Total Steel: 25 
Total Wood: 43 
Types of structures: Wood pole standoff (18), Wood pole H-Frame (4), Wood pole 
various (21), Steel lattice (20), Steel pole (5) 
Installation Date: 1923 (oldest record in Power plant) 
Conductor Clearance: Completed on both circuits 
 
The  scope of this asset condition refurbishment project includes a full aerial 
comprehensive inspection including UV and corona, steel tower climbing inspection, and 
Osmose Pole Inspection & Treatment for the wood poles. 
 
Exhibit___(EIOP-6) 
          Page 353 of 371


--- Page 504 ---
 
Significant Transmission Capital Investment 
Plan Projects and Programs 
Exhibit_(EIOP-6) 
 
Page 354 of 371 
C084554 
New Scotland-Feura Bush/New Scotland 
Long Lane ACR 
Version 1 – 
04/20/2020 
 
 
Project Justification: 
 
Age is not a determining factor for asset replacement, however age is a factor when 
ranking circuits for evaluation.  The earliest records found in Power Plant show that the 
original steel structures installed in 1923 under the Unionville-Atlantic Cement major 
location are still in service. Feura Bush-N. Catskill #2 was originally part of these lines 
prior to segmentation and is of the same vintage. During our inspections on the Feura 
Bush-N. Catskill #2, we found tracking and broken glass on many of the insulators and 
large sections of deteriorated shield wire. Testing on the shield wire showed 50% or less 
remaining strength on these sections.  
 
In the past five (5) years these circuits have had four (4) operations: one (1) being 
momentary and three (3) being lockouts. All of these events have been attributed to 
unknown causes.  
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Refurbishment of this line is necessary to provide reliable service to customers served by 
National Grid.  This overhead line refurbishment program promotes safety and reliability 
by addressing asset condition issues and allowing the transmission lines to meet the 
governing National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) under which they were built by 
replacing deteriorating structures and line components that no longer structurally or 
electrically conform to the NESC. 
 
Alternatives: 
 
The following alternatives will be considered as part of the Needs Case pending 
inspection: 
 
Alternative 1 - Targeted Refurbishment: This alternative replaces deteriorated structures, 
insulators and hardware, adds improved grounding, and targeted replacement of 
conductor and shield wire on the mainline and taps, 
 
Alternative 2 - Line Rebuild: If the conductor fails testing and it is deemed the steel 
structures are too deteriorated to remain in service, the circuit will need to be rebuilt, 
 
Alternative 3 - Smart Fault Detection and Automated Line Switching:  This is an option 
to aid in restoring customers during a lockout but will not prevent customers from 
experiencing momentary interruptions.

Alternative 4 - REV solutions: Cannot be implemented as these assets are still necessary

DER/NWA Alternative:   
 
The Company’s Non-Wires Alternative (NWA) Suitability Criteria considers the 
driver/spending rationale, timeframe, and potential costs to address a system need in 
determining whether that need can practicably be addressed with an NWA.  Since the 
justification for this project is Asset Condition in nature, it was determined that this 
project will not be evaluated for a potential NWA.

Program Name:  
N/A 
 
Associated Funding Numbers:  N/A 
 
Description: 
 
Replace 4 overdutied breakers.  
 
Project Justification: 
 
Energy Highway Project Segment A and B projects will increase fault duty in the area. 
The breakers at Leeds will exceed their interrupting duty and need to be replaced to 
handle the increase in fault current. Duty in excess of a breaker's nameplate capability 
indicates a potential for catastrophic failure if a breaker is exposed to the associated 
worst-case fault. 
 
Customer Benefit: 
 
Replacing breakers with higher interrupting capability will allow the breakers to safely 
interrupt and withstand faults. This will increase transmission system reliability, mitigate 
the risks of unwanted outages, safety and environmental concerns associated with 
equipment failure.

Alternatives: 
 
Do Nothing: this will not address the risks of unwanted outages on the transmission 
system.  
 
DER/NWA Alternative: 
 
An NWA Alternative cannot meet the need (to increase breaker interrupting duty) met by 
this project and will therefore not be considered. 
 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA):  
 
Reliability upgrades improve the system's ability to avoid a contingency (hardening, 
flood mitigation), reduce the exposure to contingency (fusing), and/or improve post 
contingency system capacity (MWh violation upgrades). Such benefits create more 
opportunities for renewable energy resources DER (such as PV and ESS) to export 
power, thereby improving the economics of individual projects. Further, improved 
reliability mitigates the need for load customers to operate backup generation, which is 
typically natural gas or petroleum fueled generation.
